hypotheses.title: update(account, makerAmount, takerAmount, collateral, referrer) lets anyone move another account's position
hypotheses.description: This overload calls `_updateMarket(account, address(0), makerAmount, takerAmount, collateral, referrer)` with `signer = address(0)`. Inside `_loadUpdateContext` the `operator` and `signer` from the factory's `authorization()` are loaded but never checked against `msg.sender` anywhere in `_update`/`InvariantLib.validate`. The 5-arg overload `update(account, amount, collateral, referrer)` is documented "No collateral movement, signer is allowed to self-send", but the `(account, makerAmount, takerAmount, collateral, referrer)` overload performs both maker and taker changes plus arbitrary collateral withdrawal (`Fixed6 collateral` can be negative) with no caller check at all. The `onlyOperator`-style gating that protects `claimFee` is simply absent for these position-collateralizing functions.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `market.update(victim, 0, hugeShort, 0, victim)` (or any maker/taker delta) directly. The order is applied to `victim`'s local position/collateral because `context.account = account` in `_loadContext` and only `msg.sender`'s `signer` was loaded and never compared. A negative `collateral` argument then triggers `token.push(msg.sender, ...)` in `_update`.
hypotheses.impact: Any account's position can be altered and its collateral withdrawn to the attacker; complete loss of user funds and total breakdown of authorization.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require that `msg.sender == account || factory.operators(account, msg.sender) || signer != address(0)` inside `_updateMarket`/`_loadForUpdate`, and for maker/taker changes require the caller to be the account, an authorized operator, or a verified signer.

hypotheses.title: update(account, newMaker, newLong, newShort, collateral, protect[, referrer]) has no caller authorization
hypotheses.description: The `public` overload `update(address account, UFixed6 newMaker, UFixed6 newLong, UFixed6 newShort, Fixed6 collateral, bool protect, address referrer)` calls `_loadForUpdate(account, address(0), referrer, address(0), 0, 0)` and never restricts who may call it. Unlike the intent/`Fill`/`Take` paths, which are gated by `verifier.verifyIntent`/`verifyTake`, and unlike `claimFee` which uses `onlyOperator`, this entry point trusts `msg.sender` implicitly. Because the caller controls `newMaker`, `newLong`, `newShort` (absolute target positions, not deltas) and `collateral`, anyone can set another account's full position and drain its collateral.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker calls `market.update(victim, 0, 0, 0, <negative collateral>, false)`, which produces an order that zeroes/overwrites victim's position and pushes collateral tokens to the attacker (`newOrder.collateral.sign() == -1` → `token.push(msg.sender, ...)`).
hypotheses.impact: Theft of all collateral held by any user in the market.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add an authorization check (account, operator, or signed message) to this overload, e.g. require `msg.sender == account || factory.operators(account, msg.sender)` before proceeding.

hypotheses.title: `_accumulateFee` subtracts makerSubtractiveFee twice from trade fee and misses takerSubtractiveFee
hypotheses.description: `result.tradeFee = result.tradeFee.add(makerFee).add(takerFee).sub(makerSubtractiveFee).sub(makerSubtractiveFee);` subtracts `makerSubtractiveFee` twice, and never subtracts `takerSubtractiveFee` (which was computed just above). So the trade fee charged to the protocol is wrong: the maker referral is double-deducted while the taker referral is never deducted from `tradeFee`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any order where a maker referral is present causes `makerFee - 2*makerSubtractiveFee` to be added to market fee; any order where a taker referral is present causes `takerFee` to be credited in full to the protocol while the subtractive portion is also credited to the referrer via `result.subtractiveFee`. This is triggered in ordinary settlement and referenced by `_response(...).marketFee`.
hypotheses.impact: Protocol takes less/more than it should depending on referral composition; specifically with a taker referral, the referrer gets credited `takerSubtractiveFee` while market still received the full `takerFee`, minting value out of the market (loss to LPs/global) and in the pure maker case subtracting value that was never accounted.
hypotheses.recommendation: Change to `sub(makerSubtractiveFee).sub(takerSubtractiveFee)`.

hypotheses.title: update(address,Fixed6,address) position-only overload lets anyone mutate any position, bypassing verifier
hypotheses.description: `update(address account, Fixed6 amount, address referrer)` calls `_updateMarket(account, msg.sender, 0, amount, Fixed6Lib.ZERO, referrer)`. The `signer` is `msg.sender` but `_loadUpdateContext` never verifies the caller is authorized for `account`; the factory-supplied `operator` field is loaded into `updateContext.operator` and never consumed by any check. So `msg.sender` need not equal `account` and need not be an operator. The unsigned `Take` overload immediately above it is signature-gated, but this one is not; any address can move any account's taker position up to a magnitude change that gets applied directly.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker repeatedly calls `market.update(victim, ±amount, referrer)`, opening unwanted exposure on the victim and triggering settlement fees / liquidation exposure to the victim. Collateral loss follows through liquidation or referral-fee accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Attacker can force positions and settlement-fee debits on arbitrary accounts, leading to liquidation of other users' collateral.
hypotheses.recommendation: Gate `update(address,Fixed6,address)` on `msg.sender == account || operator || valid signer` (as already intended via `signer`) and enforce it inside `_loadForUpdate`.

hypotheses.title: Withdrawal keeper fee is levied before verifying the signed Withdrawal message
hypotheses.description: In `withdrawWithSignature`, the keeper fee is computed and pulled from the collateral account via `_handleKeeperFee(keepConfigWithdrawal, ..., data)` BEFORE `_withdrawWithSignature` calls `verifier.verifyWithdrawal(withdrawal, signature)`. `_raiseKeeperFee` decodes `(account, withdrawal.action.maxFee)` and calls `DSU.pull(account, raisedKeeperFee)` (wrapping USDC if needed). There is no check that `withdrawal`/`signature` is valid at fee time, and `keepCollateralAccount` is not used here (the fee is raised unconditionally with `0` applicable gas so the configured withdrawal config applies). The only pre-condition is deriving the account address from `withdrawal.action.common.account`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker crafts arbitrary `Withdrawal` data with `action.common.account` set to any victim owner, any huge `action.maxFee`, and an empty/garbage `signature`. Attacker submits `withdrawWithSignature`; the fee path wraps and pulls DSU from the victim's deterministic account address into the Controller and pays the caller, then the verification of the (invalid) signature only reverts the withdrawal portion — but the fee transfer already happened in the same call before the revert, and `_handleKeeperFee` transfers to the caller inside the still-executing call. Repeat across victim accounts/rounds.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of collateral (DSU/USDC) from any collateral account by an unauthenticated caller, without a valid owner signature.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify `withdrawal` against `verifier` before raising any keeper fee (mirror the `keepCollateralAccount` pattern where verification occurs before/around fee settlement, or move `_handleKeeperFee` after `_withdrawWithSignature`).

hypotheses.title: SolverVault.rebalance allows coordinator to drain market collateral outside any checkpoint accounting
hypotheses.description: `SolverVault.rebalance(from, to, amount)` calls `from.update(address(this), 0, Fixed6Lib.from(-1, amount), address(0))` and `to.update(...)` directly, bypassing `_settleUnderlying`, `_settle`, `_checkpoint`, `_manage` and the vault's own `_saveContext`. The vault's checkpoint/global/local accounting is never updated for this movement, yet the coordinator-controlled `amount` is applied as a taker order on each market at whatever price the AMM yields. Since `Vault.update` is the path that snapshots `market.locals(address(this)).collateral` into the checkpoint and enforces `context.local.current == context.local.latest`, the direct market updates leave `_checkpoints` stale relative to actual market collateral.
hypotheses.attackPath: Coordinator (or a compromised/rotated coordinator address; see `updateCoordinator`) calls `rebalance(from, to, hugeAmount)` repeatedly to move the vault's collateral between markets through taker orders at AMM prices, generating trade fees/slippage loss on the vault, and does so outside the checkpoint cadence so `totalAssets()`/`_settle` later reconcile a different collateral than what the vault believes it holds. The taker positions created are not reflected in `MakerStrategyLib`/`SolverStrategyLib` targets until the next settle, so the following `_manage` may lever the vault against the already-moved collateral.
hypotheses.impact: Coordinator can move/lose vault funds through unrestricted taker orders and desync vault checkpoint accounting from actual market collateral, harming depositors.
hypotheses.recommendation: Route rebalance through the standard settle/checkpoint path (or at minimum perform `_settleUnderlying()` and checkpoint updates and cap `amount` by strategy targets) so vault accounting tracks every market state change.

hypotheses.title: updateOperatorWithSignature / updateSignerWithSignature reject delegated signers
hypotheses.description: Both `updateOperatorWithSignature` and `updateSignerWithSignature` (and their batch variant) require `operatorUpdate.common.signer == operatorUpdate.common.account`. However, the Verifier contract's `_authorized` accepts delegated `marketFactory.signers(account, signer)` (i.e., signers) for signing these intents. A signer legitimately encrypting/signing a SignedIntent on behalf of the account will always be rejected here because the signer != account check is hard-coded after `verifier.verifyOperatorUpdate(...)`. This means the delegated signer path for access management never works via these paths, only via direct calls. In addition, extensions cannot be used to relay access updates (since no extension-based authorization is performed in MarketFactory for these entry points).
hypotheses.attackPath: A user sets up a delegated signer to manage their access. The signer signs an `OperatorUpdate` intent. Anyone submits it to `updateOperatorWithSignature`; `verifier.verifyOperatorUpdate` passes (because signer is authorized via `marketFactory.signers(account, signer)`), but the explicit `common.signer != common.account` check reverts `MarketFactoryInvalidSignerError`.
hypotheses.impact: Delegated signers cannot perform access updates through the signature path, so account control cannot be delegated for this function class despite the verifier permitting it. Functional DoS for the delegated-signer access-management flow.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either allow `signers(account, signer)` to authorize these updates (drop the strict `signer == account` check and rely solely on `verifier.verify...`), or document and enforce that only account-signed updates are accepted in the verifier too.

hypotheses.title: Sequential overlapping commits permanently lock async settlement fees
hypotheses.description: When commit() is called for a requested version, `_commitRequested` stores the full fee response and then immediately calls `oracle.claimFee(...)` for the *total* settlement fee (sync + async) based on the current callback count. All of that fee is paid out to the factory/keeper at commit time. However, the async portion is also later re-paid per callback in `settle()` via `market.token().push(receiver, asyncFee)` for each account. Worse, the actual settlement fee is only fully earned once every callback is settled; if additional accounts register extra callbacks, or the number of callbacks at commit time differs from the number settled, the payout accounting drifts. This means async fees can be double-counted (paid at commit and per callback) or the fee pool can be over-drained relative to what the market charged, leaving later claimers (or the oracle beneficiary) underfunded.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Keeper commits a requested version with N registered callbacks; `claimFee` pays `syncFee + asyncFee*N` out of the market's accrued fees to the factory and `syncFee` to receiver. 2) `settle()` is then called, and for every one of the N accounts it pushes `asyncFee` to the receiver again (`for i < maxCount && callbacks.length() > 0`). 3) The same async fee N times is paid at commit and N times again in settle — double spend of the market fee pool.
hypotheses.impact: Oracle fee pool over-drained; the beneficiary (Oracle.sol `withdraw`) or the market can become insolvent for fee claims; keepers can drain token balance of `Oracle` via excessive `market.token().push`.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_commitRequested`, claim only `syncFee` via `oracle.claimFee`; pay `asyncFee` from the pre-funded pool during `settle`, or track already-claimed amounts.

hypotheses.title: SolverVault.rebalance bypasses pending-order invariant and can strand/over-withdraw collateral
hypotheses.description: `Vault.update` and `Vault._update` enforce `context.local.current != context.local.latest => revert VaultExistingOrderError()` and re-settle/rebalance before touching state. `SolverVault.rebalance(IMarket from, IMarket to, UFixed6 amount)` is `onlyCoordinator` and calls `from.update(address(this), 0, Fixed6Lib.from(-1, amount), 0)` and `to.update(...)` directly, without going through `_settle`, `_checkpoint`, `_manage`, or `_saveContext`, and without checking pending ids or leverage. Because the vault's market calls are made with the vault as `msg.sender`, the market accepts these orders regardless of the vault's own pending/local state, so a coordinator can drive each market's `Local.collateral` outside the invariants tracked in the vault's `_checkpoints`/`_accounts`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Coordinator (or compromised coordinator key) calls `rebalance(from, to, amount)` repeatedly to move collateral: withdraw large collateral from `from` while it has an open maker/taker position (allowed so long as market margin check passes for that order), and/or push the vault's `to` market position into a state inconsistent with the next `_checkpointAtId` snapshot. Then any user calls `update`/`settle`; `_loadContext` reads live `local.collateral` per market and `checkpoints(...)` recomputes `checkpoint.collateral` from the market, so the vault's accounted `assets`/`chargeFees` will diverge from what users expected at the time checkpoints were recorded.
hypotheses.impact: Position/leverage limits configured by the vault owner (via `updateLeverage`/`updateWeights`) are not enforced on this path, and collateral can be reallocated so that the vault's recorded checkpoint does not match live market state, enabling value extraction from other LPs or making redemption math (`toAssetsGlobal`) use inconsistent assets.
hypotheses.recommendation: Route `SolverVault.rebalance` through the same `_settleUnderlying`/`_loadContext`/`_settle`/`_manage`/`_saveContext` flow (or at least require no pending orders and enforce leverage) before forwarding the market update.

hypotheses.title: `_credit` computes liquidation fee, subtractive and solver fees from `CheckpointAccumulationResponse` but not from maker/taker value streams
hypotheses.description: In `_processOrderLocal` the three credits (`accumulationResponse.liquidationFee`, `.subtractiveFee`, `.solverFee`) are read from `CheckpointLib.accumulate`. If those fields in `CheckpointAccumulationResponse` are not strictly funded by a corresponding debit in the checkpoint/liquidation accounting, `_credit` silently credits `_locals[receiver].claimable` with tokens that were never added to the market's `total`/claims ledger. `claimFee` then pushes real tokens out of the market for `claimable` regardless of ledger consistency (see `claimFee` -> `token.push(msg.sender, ...)` for `feeReceived` including `newLocal.claimable`).
hypotheses.attackPath: If the checkpoint accumulation can be made to over-report `subtractiveFee` (e.g. via referral amounts `order.makerReferral`/`takerReferral` magnitudes that exceed the corresponding fee debit in `VersionLib._accumulateFee` — which we've shown double/missing subtraction in), the referrer's local `claimable` grows beyond what was debited from the market. Referrer calls `claimFee` and drains the token balance beyond what they're entitled to.
hypotheses.impact: Claim of DEX/market collateral exceeding contributions, causing stranded positions or loss for other users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure the credited amounts are exactly equal to amounts debited earlier in the same settlement (assert), and fix the `_accumulateFee` subtraction bug so ledger is balanced.

hypotheses.title: Rebalance loop drains DSU from account that lacks it, reverting the whole rebalance
hypotheses.description: `_rebalanceGroup` first pulls collateral from surplus markets (`imbalances[i] < 0`) and then pushes to deficit markets (`imbalances[i] > 0`). `Account.marketTransfer` for a positive amount calls `wrapIfNecessary(..., true)` which only wraps *existing USDC* in the account; if the account holds no USDC (the normal steady state, since deposits go straight to markets), DSU balance remains insufficient and `Market.update`'s `DSU.pull` reverts. Because the two loops are separate, the push loop can fail after the pull loop has already credited the account, so the keeper's whole transaction reverts and the group can never be rebalanced even though it is outside threshold.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner configures any group (targets summing to 1) and deposits all collateral into markets via `marketTransfer`. Time passes and imbalances appear. A keeper calls `rebalanceGroup(owner, group)`; `checkGroup` returns `canRebalance = true`, the pull loop settles surplus transfers, then the push loop calls `account.marketTransfer(market, positiveImbalance)`, `wrapIfNecessary` finds zero USDC, and `market.update` reverts on insufficient DSU, reverting the entire rebalance. Anyone can repeat the call and it always reverts.
hypotheses.impact: Core rebalancing (the whole point of the group feature) is permanently unusable for the common configuration where the account holds only market collateral, so positions drift out of target allocation with no way to correct them; keepers can never collect the `maxFee`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either pull surplus collateral into the account before computing pushes and let the wrap step fund positive transfers from that pulled DSU (i.e. ensure DSU balance is aggregated before pushing), or skip positive transfers when `DSU.balanceOf(account) + USDC.balanceOf(account)` is insufficient instead of reverting.

hypotheses.title: Manager.claim() transfers to msg.sender instead of the account owner
hypotheses.description: `claim(address account, bool unwrap) external onlyOperator(account, msg.sender)` withdraws `claimable[account]` and then pushes the tokens to `msg.sender` (`DSU.push(msg.sender, ...)` or `_unwrapAndWithdraw(msg.sender, ...)`), not to `account`. The `onlyOperator` modifier allows any operator (including a protocol-wide `extensions[sender]` or `marketFactory.operators(account, sender)`) to call this. Furthermore `claimable` is credited by interface fees to `order.interfaceFee.receiver` — anyone using an operator for their account, or any registered extension, can drain that receiver's accrued fee by calling claim on the receiver's address and taking funds to themselves.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker with operator rights on account (e.g. via an approved operator, or because they are a protocol `extension`) calls `claim(victim, unwrap)` where `victim` is an interface-fee receiver; the entire `claimable[victim]` is sent to the attacker. Alternatively, any operator of a user can siphon the user's claimable balance.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of accumulated DSU interface fees / claimable balances by any operator (or extension) on the owning account.
hypotheses.recommendation: Push to `account` (or to a recipient specified and authorized by the account owner), rather than to `msg.sender`.

hypotheses.title: Rebalance config dedup check reads overwritten storage, allowing duplicate markets
hypotheses.description: In `_updateRebalanceGroup`, the comment says "read from storage to trap duplicate markets in the message", but `marketToGroup[owner][message.markets[i]]` is written to `message.group` earlier in the same loop iteration. On the second occurrence of a duplicated market, `currentGroup` equals `message.group` (non-zero), which does not trigger `ControllerMarketAlreadyInGroupError`. The duplicate is pushed twice into `groupToMarkets`, and the stored config for that market is overwritten by the later config while `totalAllocation` sums both targets. This makes the loop's own comment false.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner (or delegated signer) signs a `RebalanceConfigChange` containing the same market twice, e.g. markets=[A, A], configs=[{0.05,0},{0.95,0}]. The first iteration sets `marketToGroup[A]=group`. The second iteration reads `marketToGroup[A]==group`, not 0, so no revert; config for A becomes {0.95,0} but `totalAllocation` is 1e18 and passes. `marketToGroup`/`_rebalanceConfigs` are silently overwritten while `groupToMarkets` holds A twice.
hypotheses.impact: On `rebalanceGroup`, `_queryMarketCollateral` counts A's collateral twice in `groupCollateral`, and the rebalance loops call `account.marketTransfer(A, ...)` twice for the same market. Transfers pull/push collateral twice into the same market, corrupting the owner's actual collateral and abandoning any other market that would have been assigned the intended allocation. This can leave the account over/under-collateralized compared to the signed intent and can cause unintended withdrawals/pushes from the collateral account, harming the owner.
hypotheses.recommendation: Move the duplicate check to a separate pre-pass that reads and rewrites no state, or track a per-loop "seen" mapping. Revert if `marketToGroup[owner][market] != 0` regardless of equality with `message.group`, and reject duplicate markets inside the same message.

hypotheses.title: chargeFee enabled for any market operator lets operators drain collateral account via DSU wrap
hypotheses.description: `chargeFee(owner, amount)` is gated by `onlyOperator(owner, msg.sender)` using `marketFactory.operators(owner, operator)`. Market operators are routinely granted to markets/vaults and third-party integrations (a signer/operator approval is a broad "may act on my positions" grant). Nothing limits `amount` to a fee actually assessed or caps it; an operator can call `chargeFee(victimOwner, hugeAmount)`. `wrapIfNecessary` wraps USDC in the account, and `DSU.pullTo(account, msg.sender, transferAmount)` transfers the DSU to the operator. This turns an "operate my positions" permission into full collateral withdrawal, which is broader than the operator relationship in core is meant to convey.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker obtains operator status for a victim (approved as market operator/signer via normal flows, or is a malicious market/vault the victim interacts with). Calls `chargeFee(victim, victimAccountDSU+USDC)`; account wraps remaining USDC then DSU is pulled to attacker.
hypotheses.impact: Full theft of the collateral account's DSU/USDC by anyone holding operator status for the owner, without any signed withdrawal.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only permit registered/trusted fee-charging contracts to call `chargeFee`, or require owner-signed fee authorization (amount-bound) like other actions; do not reuse market operator permission for arbitrary account debits.

hypotheses.title: Market.updateIntent charges solver but `update(address,Intent)` never verifies solver signature is the sender
hypotheses.description: In `update(address account, Intent calldata intent, bytes memory signature)` the intent is verified against `intent.common.signer`, but the maker side is built from `msg.sender` (passed as `address(0)` signer) while the taker side uses `intent.common.account`. Any caller can choose `account` and signer via the signed intent fields: since `_updateIntent` passes `intent.common.account`/`intent.common.signer` for the signer side, but the "account" side is `msg.sender` with no constraint that `msg.sender == intent.common.account`. This means the intent signer's position is mutated against an arbitrary account chosen by `msg.sender`, and `verifier.verifyIntent` only checks that the intent's own signer signed it, not that `account` is `msg.sender`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker observes a signed intent from victim signer with `common.account = X`. Attacker calls `update(attackerChosenAccount, intent, signature)`. The victim signer side is applied to `intent.common.account` (fine) but the counterparty side applies to `msg.sender` — the caller can pick any `account` argument, so the account parameter is freely chosen and unrelated to the intent, mutating an arbitrary account's position without their consent.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized position change for any account address passed as `account`, manipulating their position/collateral accounting and potentially forcing them into liquidation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `account == msg.sender` (or `account == intent.common.account`) in the `update(address,Intent,bytes)` overload, and similarly check the solver-side account in the `Fill` overload is `fill.common.account`.

hypotheses.title: OrderStorageLocal packs protection in low bits of slot2 but read uses wrong offset, inverting protection/invalidation
hypotheses.description:
In `OrderStorageLocalLib.store`, slot2 packs `makerReferral` (bits 255..192), `takerReferral` (191..128), `protection` (127), and `invalidation` (126..119). The shift math for `protection` is `uint256(newValue.protection << (256-1)) >> (256-64-64-1)`, which, for `protection = 1`, yields bit 127; for `invalidation` uses `<<(256-8) >> (256-64-64-1-8)` producing bits 118..111 — wait, the right shift of `256-64-64-1-8 = 119` leaves the bits at 119..112 in-slot. `read` extracts protection with `uint256(slot2 << (256-64-64-1)) >> (256-1)` (1-bit value at bit 127) and invalidation with `>>(256-8)` after shifting `<<(256-64-64-1-8)` (8 bits). So write and read are consistent for `protection` only if it is `0/1`. However `validate` and the store guard `newValue.protection > 1` and `newValue.invalidation > type(uint8).max` limit range but the global `OrderStorageGlobalLib.store` calls `OrderStorageLib.validate` which does NOT check protection/invalidation, and `OrderStorageGlobalLib` never stores them anyway, so the global pending aggregate read always returns protection=0, invalidation=0. But `_updateAndStore → _storeUpdateContext` writes `updateContext.orderGlobal` to storage `_pendingOrder[...]` even though `OrderStorageGlobalLib.store` silently drops `protection`/`invalidation`; in `_update`, aggregate global pending `context.pendingGlobal.add(newOrder)` adds protection counts to the aggregate in-memory order, and then `_storeContext` persists via `_pending.store(...)`. That persistence path is fine for `Order` with protection in-memory only. However on a later reload, `pendingGlobal.protection` is 0 even though orderGlobal's protection is needed; the "protection" aggregate counter is used by `context.pendingGlobal` for downstream invariants.
Rewrite: in-memory `context.pendingGlobal` carries `protection` but the aggregate global pending *stored* struct (`OrderStorageGlobal`) cannot represent `protection`/`invalidation` at all (slot 2 only has referrals per the comment). Any logic relying on `context.pendingGlobal.protection`/`invalidation` after a reload will see stale zero. This is a real semantic gap; if `InvariantLib` or anything else inspects pending global's protection, it will misbehave.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker opens a protected order, it is stored to `_pending`, protection gets lost on store. On a subsequent `settle`, pendingGlobal is reloaded with `protection = 0`, so any invariant that assumed protected liquidity is not enforced.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of protection guarantees; positions opened as "protected" may be liquidatable while protection was assumed.
hypotheses.recommendation: Persist protection and invalidation in the aggregate global order slot, or ensure readers never rely on `pendingGlobal.protection/invalidation` after a store/reload.

hypotheses.title: `Oracle.claimFee` pushes settlement fee to `msg.sender` but charged from market balance, allowing sub-oracle to claim arbitrary amount
hypotheses.description: `claimFee` accepts any `settlementFeeRequested` and pushes that amount of market token to `msg.sender` via `market.token().push`. The actual pull is `market.claimFee(address(this))` which returns `feeReceived`. `feeReceived.sub(settlementFeeRequested)` reverts underflow if `settlementFeeRequested > feeReceived`, but if the market has pre-funded fees above what the sub-oracle's store computed, the sub-oracle factory can request more than its own store authorized—`claimFee` has no check tying `settlementFeeRequested` to a per-version value it computed. The only guard is the underflow.
hypotheses.attackPath: A registered sub-oracle (which is a KeeperOracle factory) can call `claimFee(X)` with X up to `feeReceived` even if the intended settlement fee for the version was smaller, siphoning fees that should go to the beneficiary. The beneficiary's remainder is only `feeReceived - settlementFeeRequested`.
hypotheses.impact: Sub-oracle factory can drain all outstanding market fees, leaving the beneficiary nothing.
hypotheses.recommendation: Bound `settlementFeeRequested` to the value computed by the sub-oracle for the committed version (e.g., pass it through and verify), or cap by `feeReceived` less a beneficiary reserve.

hypotheses.title: commit() pays settlement fee computed from callback count that can change afterward
hypotheses.description: The receipt used during `commit` is `priceResponse.toOracleReceipt(_localCallbacks[version.timestamp].length())`, which captures whatever callback count exists at commit time. But the settlement fee is claimed upfront while `settle()` pays out per callback based on whatever remains in `_localCallbacks[version]`. Because callbacks may be added after commit but before the loop finishes (or not be settled if `maxCount` is too low), the number of async fees actually paid (per callback) does not match the number charged at commit. Fees can be undercharged (beneficiary loses revenue) or over-claimed relative to callbacks actually processed.
hypotheses.attackPath: Keeper commits with `maxCount`/callback set length L; `claimFee` charges sync + async*L; but only some of the L entries are ever settled (e.g., someone stops calling settle, or extra accounts are added later). Beneficiary either over- or under-paid depending on drift.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect fee distribution; beneficiary loses fee revenue; market can end with unsettled fees stuck/unrecoverable; oracle irrecoverably out of balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute and claim settlement fee from the *final* number of callbacks (e.g., charge per callback in `settle` instead of committing async fee upfront).

hypotheses.title: Account.deposit() pulls USDC only, but deploy/controller path assumes DSU collateral; deposit yields untracked USDC
hypotheses.description: `Account.deposit(amount)` merely does `USDC.pull(msg.sender, amount)`, leaving raw USDC in the account with no DSU minted and no bookkeeping. `marketTransfer` and `withdraw` assume DSU / wrap-if-necessary semantics, and `wrapIfNecessary` only wraps when DSU is short and USDC balance is non-zero at call time. Users who hold USDC in the account (via `deposit`) get nothing recorded; their funds sit idle and become reachable by whoever can trigger `wrap`/`unwrap` operations on that account (owner or controller via a signed action). Since `ownerOrController` permits `factory()` (=Controller) to call `wrap`, `wrapIfNecessary`, and `unwrap`, any controller-executed action (e.g. a `chargeFee` or rebalance triggered by an operator) can consume/wrap the idle USDC belonging to the owner, and `withdraw(amount, shouldUnwrap)` computes `USDC.balanceOf()` and pushes `amount` even if the owner meant to keep DSU.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner calls `deposit`; later a controller path (signature-authorized marketTransfer with positive amount → `wrapIfNecessary`/`wrap`) wraps the deposited USDC and the account's DSU is consumed by market.update; or `withdraw(..., false)` sends the USDC out while DSU accounting is untouched. Operator-initiated `chargeFee` can also pull against the wrapped balance.
hypotheses.impact: Loss/misappropriation of owner's deposited USDC and confusing collateral accounting between USDC and DSU.
hypotheses.recommendation: Make `deposit` wrap USDC into DSU immediately (or restrict it to wrap on deposit), and/or require the owner to explicitly wrap; do not leave raw USDC that any ownerOrController action can convert/spend.

hypotheses.title: Coordinator.claimFee pushes entire contract token balance to comptroller, not the claimed amount — any market fee stranded in the contract is swept to comptroller
hypotheses.description: `claimFee` calls `market.claimFee(address(this))` then `market.token().push(comptroller)`. `Token18.push(receiver)` pushes the **entire** token balance held by the Coordinator, not just the newly claimed fee. If for any reason the Coordinator holds other token balances of that token (e.g., from an earlier claim to a different config, donations sent to the contract, or claiming an additional market that shares the same token), the entire balance is sent to comptroller. More importantly, if `market.token()` is a token with balances for multiple markets, claiming one market sweeps balances owed to others to comptroller immediately, which can be intended (same comptroller) but any tokens accidentally sent to the Coordinator are lost to comptroller without owner control.
hypotheses.attackPath: Anyone sends tokens to Coordinator; comptroller (or anyone via comptroller) calls claimFee and the donation is swept.
hypotheses.impact: Donated/misfunded tokens swept to comptroller; potentially funds earmarked for another market are swept because balances aren't per-market.
hypotheses.recommendation: Track the claimed amount returned by `market.claimFee`, or compare balance before/after and push only the delta.

hypotheses.title: Duplicate market in RebalanceConfigChange not detected despite comment claiming it is
hypotheses.description: The code comment says "read from storage to trap duplicate markets in the message", but it reads `message.configs[i].target` (memory) instead of `_rebalanceConfigs[owner][group][market]`, so duplicates are not trapped. When the same market appears twice, `marketToGroup` is set to the same group, the second iteration passes the `currentGroup != 0` check (it equals `message.group`), and `groupToMarkets` gets the same `IMarket` pushed twice with independent configs. `totalAllocation` can then sum to 1 by splitting the target across two identical market entries.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner signs a `RebalanceConfigChange` with `markets = [M, M]`, `configs = [{0.5, e}, {0.5, e}]`, `group = 1`. `_updateRebalanceGroup` pushes `M` twice, both with target 0.5. On a later `_rebalanceGroup`, `_queryMarketCollateral` counts M's collateral twice in `groupCollateral` and computes two imbalances against the same position; the pull loop executes one transfer and the push loop might execute another on the same market, moving collateral twice per rebalance.
hypotheses.impact: Collateral can be over-moved out of a market (the same market counted as both surplus and deficit target), and `checkGroup` bookkeeping is wrong, allowing value to be pushed/pulled unexpectedly; the per-group `maxFee` accounting is also off.
hypotheses.recommendation: Read the previous value from storage before writing (`uint256 currentGroup = marketToGroup[owner][message.markets[i]];` is present but the target accumulation should use `_rebalanceConfigs[...]` or explicitly reject duplicates by checking `marketToGroup` against the same group index or by tracking seen markets in a local set).

hypotheses.title: MarketTransfer positive amount wraps entire USDC balance, pulling more user USDC than declared
hypotheses.description: For a deposit (`amount > 0`), `marketTransfer` calls `wrapIfNecessary(UFixed18Lib.from(amount.abs()), true)`, which wraps *all* USDC held by the account rather than just the shortfall (`amount - DSU.balanceOf()`). If the account holds both DSU and USDC, a market transfer of size `amount` can mint DSU far exceeding `amount` and deposit only `amount` to the market, leaving the surplus DSU idle in the account. Any signed `MarketTransfer` thus converts more user USDC to DSU than the amount signed for.
hypotheses.attackPath: User deposits USDC via `deposit`, holds USDC in account, also has small DSU balance. A relayer submits `MarketTransfer{amount: X}` where `X > DSU.balanceOf()`. `wrapIfNecessary(X, true)` wraps `USDC.balanceOf()` (possibly > `X - DSU`) into DSU; `market.update` pulls only `X`. The extra DSU sits in the account. If this coincides with an `unwrap`-driven withdrawal flow, the user can be forced to pay more wrapping than signed.
hypotheses.impact: A signed message produces an effect larger than signed (all USDC wrapped), and the surplus is parked in the account in a form the owner cannot easily recover without a separate signed action; if the user intended to keep USDC as a stable balance they lose that option for the full balance until another action. For accounts using operators, this means a keeper/operator can force-wrap the entire USDC balance for any posiive transfer.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `marketTransfer`, wrap only the shortfall: `wrapIfNecessary(UFixed18Lib.from(amount.abs()).sub(DSU.balanceOf().min(UFixed18Lib.from(amount.abs()))), false)` or compute `wrapAmount = amountDSU > dsuBalance ? amountDSU - dsuBalance : 0` and wrap exactly that.

hypotheses.title: Trigger order execution uses stale limit price; keeper fee charged via user maxFee cap can exceed remaining collateral
hypotheses.description: `_chargeInterfaceFee` is called before `order.execute`, and `order.notionalValue` reads `market.oracle().latest().price`, so the fee is based on the current oracle price rather than the underlying execution. More importantly, `_raiseKeeperFee` in `_handleKeeperFee` pulls `min(computedFee, maxFee)` DSU from the user's collateral account via `controller.chargeFee` after the order has already run; if the collateral was fully consumed by the market update (e.g. a close that reduces collateral), `chargeFee` will revert and the whole execution fails, permanently blocking the order for a user whose collateral got tight.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user places a trigger order with `maxFee > 0` and low collateral; a keeper triggers `executeOrder` after the position has lost collateral; `_collateralAccountWithdraw(account, raisedKeeperFee)` reverts, reverting the entire execution, so the order can never execute at exactly the moment it matters (risk reduction).
hypotheses.impact: DoS of legitimate risk-reducing triggers, or forcing users to keep excess collateral in the account, which can be exploited by a keeper who delays execution until collateral is thin.
hypotheses.recommendation: Charge the keeper fee from a pre-funded balance rather than the same collateral account, or allow the fee to be capped at the account's actual available collateral and not revert the execution.

hypotheses.title: Trigger order execute reads trigger with stale oracle price, keeper controls execution timing
hypotheses.description: `executeOrder` first calls `checkOrder` which calls `order.canExecute(market.oracle().latest())` and then executes the order via `order.execute(market, account)`. The trigger decision is based on the single `latest()` price returned by the oracle, but the actual market settlement in `market.settle`/`market.update` may settle at a different (or newer) oracle version, and a keeper chooses the exact block in which to submit. Because execution is permissionless and the keeper is compensated, a keeper can select the block where the price passes the threshold and then the trade executes at the settlement price, which can move adversely between trigger and fill. The user's `price` comparison provides no slippage protection on the fill price.
hypotheses.attackPath: User places a `comparison=1 (gte)` long trigger at price P. Keeper waits until the oracle `latest()` reports a price >= P, calls `executeOrder`; meanwhile the oracle price that the market actually settles against is favorable to the opposite side (or the keeper's own position), so the user's `delta` is executed at a worse price than trigger. Keeper repeatedly does this across users. Alternatively the price spikes above P briefly, keeper executes at the top, then price reverts, leaving the user long at the peak.
hypotheses.impact: Users' trigger orders fill at prices worse than trigger/limit; predictable value extraction by keepers/MEV searchers from every trigger order.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add a user-supplied limit/slippage bound on the fill price (or on the resulting collateral) enforced in `TriggerOrderLib.execute` against the settled price, and reject execution if the settled price deviates beyond the bound.

hypotheses.title: Signed trigger-order intents reuse nonces across verifier instances and never bind the target Manager
hypotheses.description: The EIP-712 domain is statically initialized as ("Perennial V2 Trigger Orders", "1.0.0") without chainId/salt binding added in this code, and MessageProcessor.validateAndCancel(action.common,...) enforces nonce/group/expiry only against OrderVerifier's own internal state. The Manager does not verify that request.action.market or the receiving Manager matches what the signer intended beyond Action.market (which is included) — but the signature is validated by verifying `action.common.signer` while the account in `action.common.account` is used to store orders (in Manager `_placeOrder(request.action.market, request.action.common.account, ...)`). The verifier's `_authorized(account, signer)` accepts `marketFactory.signers(account, signer)`, so an authorized signer can place orders for an account, but there is no differentiator that a signature intended for one deployed OrderVerifier (or one chain, if deployed to multiple chains with the same domain) cannot be replayed on another deployment.
hypotheses.attackPath: A signer authorizes a PlaceOrderAction for account A on Manager X. A relayer (or anyone who sees the signed payload, since it is passed as calldata to PlaceOrder on the destination) submits the same payload to a Manager Y (same OrderVerifier or a redeployed verifier on a sister chain) — the domain separator matches and nonce bookkeeping is per-verifier, so the message is accepted again for account A on another market/manager.
hypotheses.impact: Signed intents can be executed more than once (per deployment), forced into orders the signer did not authorize for that destination, and replayed cross-chain / cross-manager.
hypotheses.recommendation: Include chainId, the Manager address, and the verifying contract in the domain separator (or include a per-manager nonce/verifier address hash in the struct hash), and/or track executor-per-intent in the Manager.

hypotheses.title: `executeOrder` state store after external `market.update` may re-enter and double-execute / double-charge
hypotheses.description: `executeOrder` calls `checkOrder` (view), then `_chargeInterfaceFee` which calls `controller.chargeFee` (external), then `order.execute(market, account)` which calls `market.settle` and `market.update` (external, potentially to another contract). Only after all external calls is `order.isSpent = true` written to storage. There is no reentrancy guard on `Manager`. A malicious market or a reentrant call during `market.update` (if `account` is a contract) could reenter `executeOrder` for the same orderId while `isSpent` is still false, causing double execution and double interface fee invoicing via `claimable[receiver]`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker deploys a market or participates in a market where one of the triggered interactions re-enters `Manager.executeOrder` with the same (market, account, orderId). Since `_orders[...].read()` still returns `isSpent == false`, `checkOrder` passes, `_chargeInterfaceFee` withdraws again, and `order.execute` calls `market.update` again, mutating position and inflating `claimable`.
hypotheses.impact: Double-spend of trigger order effect and double interface fee theft from the victim collateral account; corrupted keeper accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: Set `order.isSpent = true` and store before any external call (checks-effects-interactions), and/or add a `nonReentrant` modifier to `executeOrder`.

hypotheses.title: Coordinator rotation permanently bricks SolverVault signer/operator and lets old coordinator remain signer
hypotheses.description: updateCoordinator() calls marketFactory().updateSigner(coordinator, false) unconditionally before checking whether the current coordinator is set, and then adds newCoordinator as signer. On first use after initialization, coordinator is address(0), so this calls updateSigner(address(0), false). More importantly, the signer is updated on the market factory for the vault's account context but there is no path to revoke a previously set coordinator if updateSigner reverts/succeeds differently; when the vault is paused or the coordinator is changed twice quickly, the signature granted to the intermediate coordinator is never revoked because super.updateCoordinator(newCoordinator) sets storage only after the signer updates. The ordering means if updateSigner(newCoordinator, true) succeeds but a later step in the tx reverts, the signer change is rolled back only if the revert propagates — but if the factory's updateSigner is the external side effect and the final broadcast to market factory is incomplete, a stale authorized signer persists.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner calls updateCoordinator(A) then updateCoordinator(B): A is added as signer, then B is added and A is attempted-removed. If Vault.coordinator was previously zero (no update), first call passes address(0). A coordinator whose signer approval was never revoked can continue to sign solver trades on the vault account.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized/old coordinator keeps or gains signer authority over the vault's market positions, enabling them to trade on behalf of the vault after being replaced.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only call updateSigner when coordinator != address(0), and revoke the previous signer explicitly; consider reverting if a revoke fails.

hypotheses.title: Liquidation fee accumulation uses total settlement fee instead of only invalidated order's fees
hypotheses.description: `_accumulateLiquidationFee` sets `liquidationFee = settlementFee.mul(riskParameter.liquidationFee)` and decrements `next.liquidationFee` by that value, where `settlementFee` is `context.toOracleReceipt.settlementFee` — the total settlement fee for the oracle version. It is not multiplied/limited by the number of orders actually being invalidated/liquidated in this accumulation (unlike `_accumulateSettlementFee`, which subtracts `context.guarantee.orders`). The `next.liquidationFee` accumulator is later scaled by the local position in `CheckpointLib`, but the raw amount decremented here represents a per-version, aggregate liquidation fee value applied globally rather than conditioned on an actual liquidation event.
hypotheses.attackPath: The `liquidationFee` accumulator records a hypothetical liquidation fee proportional to the *total* version settlement fee even for versions with no liquidation. When the checkpoint later applies `liquidationFee` to a liquidated position, the accumulator value has been decremented by the full aggregate settlement-fee-scaled amount, letting the credited liquidation fee (`_credit(..., accumulationResponse.liquidationFee)`) be larger than one liquidation fee's worth of that specific order's settlement fees.
hypotheses.impact: Liquidation fees credited to liquidators can exceed what is owed for the liquidated order, draining the market's fee pool / other users' claimable value.
hypotheses.recommendation: Scale the liquidation fee by the order/settlement fee actually attributable to the liquidated order (e.g., use the per-order settlement fee via `settlementFee` divided by order count, or the order's own settlement fee) rather than the entire version total.

hypotheses.title: update(Fill,...) cross-checks solver and trader but msg.sender is never bound to solver
hypotheses.description: `update(Fill, traderSignature, solverSignature)` verifies `fill.intent` against `traderSignature` and `fill` against `solverSignature`, then applies the solver leg to `fill.common.account` and the trader leg to `fill.intent.common.account`. There is no check that `msg.sender == fill.common.account` (the solver) or that `msg.sender` is otherwise related to the solver. If the solver signature is not bound to the caller (or is a "one of" signature valid for any relayer by design), any third party can submit a solver/trader-matched fill pair; more importantly because `_updateIntent` for the trader subsequently uses `intent.common.signer` and the solver's `common.signer`, the delegation outcome depends entirely on `verifier.verifyFill` binding the fill to `msg.sender` which is not shown. Without that binding the fill can be replayed or executed by an unauthorized party.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker observes a signed Fill (trader + solver) in the mempool after it fails/expires, or copies it from calldata; resubmits it if the fill signature domain/nonce doesn't include the solver's msg.sender. The intent executions complete against `i ntent.common.account` and `fill.common.account` regardless of caller.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized execution of intents and duplicate intent fills for the trader/solver pair.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `msg.sender == fill.common.account` (or the address recovered from `solverSignature`), and ensure `verifyFill` binds signer, nonce, and this market's domain.

hypotheses.title: Fee maximum scaling can be bypassed / mismatched between commit and settle callback counting
hypotheses.description: In `_commitRequested`, `priceResponse.applyFeeMaximum` scales `syncFee` and `asyncFee` based on the callback count at commit time (`_localCallbacks[oracleVersion.timestamp].length()`). However, `settle()` reads the stored `asyncFee` per callback and pushes it for each callback actually processed, while the total fee already claimed via `oracle.claimFee(...)` was computed at commit time. New accounts can be added to `_localCallbacks[version]` after the commit through `request()` for the same timestamp (request only dedupes on `requests[_global.currentIndex]`, the callback set add always executes), so the number of callbacks processed in `settle` can exceed the count used for scaling, causing `asyncFee * actualCallbacks` to exceed `maxSettlementFee` and to exceed the amount reclaimed from the market.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker causes a request on timestamp T with few accounts (commit happens, fees scaled per small count). 2) Additional accounts call into flow that invokes `KeeperOracle.request` for the same timestamp T (adds to `_localCallbacks[T]` without new price request). 3) `settle(T, largeMaxCount, receiver)` iterates and pushes `asyncFee` for each extra account, paying out more total async fee than was accounted for in `claimFee`.
hypotheses.impact: The keeper/factory is paid more settlement fee than was claimed from the market, draining the oracle's token balance and overpaying fees relative to the cap.
hypotheses.recommendation: Snapshot the callback count used for `applyFeeMaximum` and use the same count in `settle`, or disallow adding callbacks to a version after it has been committed.

hypotheses.title: `Oracle.update` / `request` epoch switch allows timestamp regression of latest
hypotheses.description: `request` writes `oracles[_global.current].timestamp = uint96(currentTimestamp)` where `currentTimestamp` is the provider's current timestamp, which can be less than the previously stored timestamp if the new provider reports a smaller current. `_latestStale` then compares against this potentially regressed value. Also `_updateCurrent` writes `uint96(newProvider.current())` without checking it exceeds `oracles[_global.current].timestamp`. A new provider reporting a lower `current()` than the outgoing provider's recorded timestamp allows a version discontinuity where `at()` for those timestamps resolves to the new (empty) provider, returning a zero price with `valid=false`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner calls `OracleFactory.update` with new provider whose `current()` is less than old `timestamp`; queries for the gap period resolve against the new provider where no data exists, returning invalid/zero versions that can flow into market settlement.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect oracle versions for a time window; potential mis-settlement.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reject `newProvider.current()` that is less than the existing epoch timestamp, and clamp `timestamp` updates monotonically.

hypotheses.title: Oracle.claimFee pays msg.sender with token.push before validating sub-oracle still current
hypotheses.description: `claimFee` is `onlySubOracle`, which accepts either the current or the latest provider (`oracles[_global.current].provider` OR `oracles[_global.latest].provider`). During the transition window (current != latest), the old provider can still call `claimFee`, and the function pushes the settlement fee to `msg.sender` (`token.push(msg.sender, ...)`). Any provider that has ever been the `latest` during a transition, even if being deprecated, can drain fee pool. This is exploitable because the settlement is computed from a snapshot in `KeeperOracle`, so the deprecated provider can claim arbitrarily often without synchronizing with the current one.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Owner calls `Oracle.update(newProvider)` (via OracleFactory). 2) `_global.current != _global.latest` until sync. 3) The old provider (`oracles[_global.latest].provider`, e.g., a KeeperOracle) calls `claimFee` — passes `onlySubOracle` — and receives funds.
hypotheses.impact: Fees migratable to a deprecated provider; potential over-claim by stale provider if it re-calls `claimFee` in the same epoch.
hypotheses.recommendation: Restrict `claimFee` to `oracles[_global.current].provider` only, not latest.

hypotheses.title: Account.marketTransfer approves market then wraps all USDC when deposit; a malicious "market" approved via relaying? No: verified. But Controller allows arbitrary market address with DSU token only
hypotheses.description: `_marketTransferWithSignature` validates only `market.token().eq(DSU)`. It does not check that `market` is a known instance of `marketFactory`. An attacker (or any user for their own account) can pass an arbitrary contract implementing `token()` returning DSU and `update(...)` that pulls DSU from the account via the approval set in `Account.marketTransfer` (`DSU.approve(address(market))`). For the account owner's own signed message this is fine (owner chooses). But `rebalanceGroup` calls `account.marketTransfer` on markets stored in `groupToMarkets` — those were set via signed `RebalanceConfigChange`, so also owner-controlled. And `wrapIfNecessary` — the approval `DSU.approve(address(market))` is set to whatever market; a malicious market that was previously approved can later pull without further authorization (unbounded approval persists). That's a real risk: any market ever configured keeps unlimited DSU spending approval on the account, so if a market is compromised/upgraded, it can drain the account DSU. Approval is set and never revoked to the prior market after removal from group.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner adds market M to a rebalance group (M is legit instance). Over time M is upgraded (or is owned by third party). M calls `DSU.transferFrom(account, ...)` for full balance because `Account.marketTransfer` did `DSU.approve(address(M))` with no amount and it is never reset. Removal from group does not reset.
hypotheses.impact: Stale unlimited DSU approvals to markets allow a previously-approved market to later drain account DSU, far exceeding what was intended to be transferred.
hypotheses.recommendation: Approve exact `amount` inside `marketTransfer` instead of unlimited approval (Token18.approve with amount), clearing afterwards; or restrict approvals to known factory instances and reset.

hypotheses.title: Withdraw can silently leave funds in the account when amount is UFixed6.MAX
hypotheses.description: When `amount == UFixed6.MAX` and `shouldUnwrap`, `unwrapAmount = DSU.balanceOf()` but `unwrap` is capped implicitly: `unwrap(DSU.balanceOf())` calls `reserve.redeem`, which returns USDC that may be less than DSU redeemed if the reserve applies fees, but more importantly the subsequent `pushAmount = USDC.balanceOf()` pushes all USDC held by the account, so any DSU the reserve did not redeem (e.g., partial redemption, prior rejected DSU) stays behind. More critically, when `shouldUnwrap == false` and `amount == UFixed6.MAX`, only `USDC.balanceOf()` is pushed and all DSU is left in the account, contradicting the documented "full withdrawal" semantics of `UFixed6.MAX` and stranding DSU.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner signs `Withdrawal{amount: UFixed6.MAX, unwrap: false}`. `WithdrawalLib.hash` includes the flag but `Controller.withdrawWithSignature` → `account.withdraw(UFixed6.MAX, false)` skips the unwrap branch and pushes only `USDC.balanceOf()`; the DSU balance remains in the Account contract with no mechanism for the owner (only ownerOrController) to recover more than what the same "full" message would withdraw.
hypotheses.impact: A user intending to fully exit is left with a stranded DSU balance in the account; any subsequent full-withdraw attempt requires a new signed message, and if the owner loses signing access (or uses a one-shot off-chain signer) those DSU tokens are effectively lost.
hypotheses.recommendation: When `amount == UFixed6.MAX`, always unwrap the entire DSU balance to USDC (or push DSU to owner when `shouldUnwrap` is false), so "full withdrawal" leaves zero balance in the account.

hypotheses.title: InvariantLib returns early for protected orders, skipping operator/collateral checks that protected path relies on
hypotheses.description: For protected (liquidation) orders, the function returns after checking protection and price deviation, skipping margin, efficiency, liquidity, and `context.local.collateral < 0` checks. `Market.settle`/`update` rely on these invariants for non-protected orders, so a liquidator-triggered path can leave collateralized debt if the liquidator's local position accounting wasn't already validated; combined with `_validateProtection` allowing `newOrder.collateral == 0` and `newOrder.isEmpty()`, the protected path doesn't force a full close in all cases beyond the ones enumerated.
hypotheses.attackPath: A caller invokes the liquidation path with a `newOrder` that `protected()` returns true for, but whose effect is a partial close and zero collateral; the invariant that margin be maintained post-update is skipped for the resulting local position (as long as `currentPositionLocal` is single-sided and pending crosses zero per `_validateProtection`), leaving an under-collateralized position on the books.
hypotheses.impact: Under-collateralized positions can persist after liquidation, allowing bad debt to accumulate and be socialized to other users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either enforce post-liquidation margin (or a stricter health bound) explicitly for the protected path, or confirm via tests that `context.local.collateral < 0` is guaranteed to be checked on the subsequent non-protected update of the same account.

hypotheses.title: MarketFactory.authorization considers extensions as operators for any account, including collateral withdrawal via operator routes
hypotheses.description: `authorization` returns `account == sender || extensions[sender] || operators[account][sender]`. Extensions therefore have operator privileges on every account. In `Market`, an operator can modify collateral (e.g. withdraw to the account holder through `claimable`, or the `MultiInvoker` routes). Combined with any extension bug or upgrade, an extension (or compromise thereof) can redirect collateral or open positions for any account. The comment says extensions have operator privileges, but the design grants full financial control rather than scoped action rights.
hypotheses.attackPath: An admin adds/keeps any extension; a vulnerability in an extension (or an admin mistake / malicious extension) lets it call into Market as operator for any account and withdraw or trade against their collateral.
hypotheses.impact: Global account compromise for every account interacting with any extension; user funds at risk from extension bugs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Do not grant extensions universal operator authority for collateral-withdrawing operations; instead limit extension powers to order placement/pending cancellation and require account consent for collateral moves.

hypotheses.title: claim() lets operator unwrap and withdraw to msg.sender, but claimable is per-account; operator of one account can direct funds to themselves
hypotheses.description: `claim(address account, bool unwrap)` is guarded by `onlyOperator(account, msg.sender)` and sends the unwrapped DSU/USDC to `msg.sender` (`_unwrapAndWithdraw(msg.sender, ...)` and `DSU.push(msg.sender, ...)`) rather than to `account`. The `claimable[account]` balance belongs to the account owner. Any operator that the account has approved (which includes any address the owner enabled through `updateOperator`, and any protocol `extension`) can call `claim(owner, false/true)` and route the owner's claimable DSU/USDC to the operator's own address. Operators are expected to be able to update positions but the intent of `claimable` is the owner's funds.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Account approves malicious/mistaken operator via `updateOperator(malicious, true)`. 2) Owner accumulates `claimable[owner]` from interface fees. 3) Malicious operator calls `claim(owner, true)`, gets the unwrapped USDC at `msg.sender`. Similarly any protocol `extensions[]` address can pull any user's claimable instantly.
hypotheses.impact: Theft of all claimable fees of an account by any operator/extension; protocol extensions get sweeping power over arbitrary users' claimable balances.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `claim`, transfer to `account` always (or to msg.sender only if `msg.sender == account`), so operators cannot redirect the funds.

hypotheses.title: Interface fee percentage can exceed account collateral / maxFee; no cap and computed from pre-settle position
hypotheses.description: When `interfaceFee.fixedFee` is false, `feeAmount = order.notionalValue(market, account) * order.interfaceFee.amount`. `notionalValue` computes the delta times the latest price; if `delta == MAGIC_VALUE_CLOSE_POSITION` it returns the full position magnitude times price. The resulting `feeAmount` can be arbitrarily large (e.g. proportional fee on a huge position close), and there is no cap against the account's actual collateral or against `order.maxFee`. `_collateralAccountWithdraw` then calls `controller.chargeFee(account, feeAmount)`, which (depending on Controller) may withdraw directly from the account's collateral and can drain the account or revert. `isValid`/`store` only bound `interfaceFee.amount` to uint64, not to a percentage <=1; `interfaceFee.amount` is a UFixed6 but can be >1 (e.g. 5e6 for 5x) since only `store` bounds it by uint64 max.
hypotheses.attackPath: Account (or signed action) places a trigger order with `interfaceFee.amount > 1` (e.g., UFixed6 of 2.0) and `fixedFee=false`. On execution, `_chargeInterfaceFee` withdraws `2x notional` from the account via `controller.chargeFee`, potentially draining the account (if controller permits) or causing DoS of execution. Keeper/relayer who placed the fee receiver gets the inflated fee.
hypotheses.impact: User funds can be drained (through interface fee `amount > 1`) or the trigger order becomes unexecutable (DoS) because the fee exceeds collateral.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `interfaceFee.amount <= 1e6 (100%)` in `store/placeOrder` when `fixedFee == false`, and cap the computed fee against the account's available collateral and `order.maxFee`.

hypotheses.title: SolverStrategyLib._allocateMarket under-allocates collateral when markets count > 0 and can revert on rounding
hypotheses.description: `_allocateValue` returns `amount.div(UFixed6Lib.from(markets))` when `latestCollateral.isZero()`; `UFixed6.div` truncates. In `allocate`, the residual `newCollateral.sub(allocatedCollateral)` is added only to `targets[0].collateral`, but `newMarketAssets` used for the leverage cap in each market is computed from the truncated per-market allocation, and `target.taker` is derived from `newMarketAssets` while `target.collateral` is derived from `newMarketCollateral`. On the first deposit with many markets, the individual allocations can sum to less than `newCollateral`, and each market's `newMarketAssets` may be less than `minMargin`, forcing `newMarketAssets = 0` for all markets even though the aggregate would satisfy minimums.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner registers many markets; first depositor deposits just above the `minDeposit`; each market receives `newCollateral / markets` which, due to truncation and `minMargin` check against the per-market slice, evaluates below `minMargin`, setting all `newMarketAssets` to zero and skipping deployment. Conversely if the residual is added to `targets[0].collateral` after `_allocateMarket` has already computed that market's `newMarketAssets` and `target.taker`, market 0 gets extra collateral without a corresponding taker, which is later re-balanced by `rebuild`.
hypotheses.impact: First-deposit allocation is systematically miscomputed and can permanently mint an unbacked `targets[0].collateral` delta that does not match the leverage calculation, leaving the vault over-collateralized in market 0 and under-deployed elsewhere; on small deposits it can also trigger repeated `SolverStrategyPendingTradeError` reverts that block deposits.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the residual per-market before deriving `newMarketAssets` and `target.taker`, or add residual to `newMarketCollateral`/`newMarketAssets` of market 0 before computing `maxMagnitude`.

hypotheses.title: MakerStrategyLib._loadContext reads `latestPrice` without validity check, allowing zero/degenerate price to distort `newMaker`
hypotheses.description: `_loadContext` sets `marketContext.latestPrice = latestVersion.price` from `registration.market.oracle().latest()` without checking `latestVersion.valid` (unlike `oracle.status()`'s `current`/`latest` distinction used in `Vault._loadContext`). `_allocateMarket` computes `marketAssets.muldiv(leverage, marketContext.latestPrice.abs())`, so if the latest oracle version is invalid or its price is zero (e.g., a market whose oracle has not yet produced a valid version), `newMaker` can be computed against price 0 (reverting on `muldiv` by zero) or against a stale/zero mark, producing wildly wrong `target.maker`.
hypotheses.attackPath: Vault owner registers a market whose oracle has an invalid latest version (a normal state that can occur between oracle versions). Any call to `rebalance`/`update` then either reverts in `muldiv` (DoS on the vault path) or produces a target that exceeds the intended leverage, which the market will accept if margin permits.
hypotheses.impact: DoS of deposits/withdrawals/rebalance on MakerVault, or over-sized maker positions from an invalid oracle version, reducing solvency of the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reject or skip allocation for markets with `latestVersion.valid == false`, matching `Vault._loadContext`'s reliance on `oracle().status()`.

hypotheses.title: Checkpoint._calculateProfitShare uses `assets` which can be below previous mark, producing `newMark.sub(mark)` underflow protection reliance and possible zero-share profit
hypotheses.description: `newMark = mark.max(assets/shares)` then `profitAssets = profitShare * (newMark - mark) * shares`. If `assets` are negative (insolvent checkpoint), `UFixed18Lib.from(UFixed6Lib.unsafeFrom(self.assets))` wraps the negative Fixed6 as a huge UFixed18, so `assets/shares` overflows to a very large number, making `newMark` huge and `profitShares` enormous (or reverting on the muldiv). `complete` calls this before checking anything. This path is reachable whenever a checkpoint becomes insolvent (assets <= 0), which `unhealthy()` explicitly acknowledges can happen.
hypotheses.attackPath: A market loss makes `self.assets` negative in the next checkpoint (e.g., vault holds a losing maker position). `_calculateProfitShare` is called during `_settle`; `unsafeFrom` on the negative `Fixed6` produces a near-2^256 value, so the computed mark/profitShares are garbage; best case the mark is inflated and shares minted to the coordinator, worst case it reverts and blocks all settlement.
hypotheses.impact: Settlement of the vault can be permanently bricked during insolvency, locking user funds; or inflated shares minted to the coordinator, diluting users.
hypotheses.recommendation: Short-circuit `_calculateProfitShare` when `self.assets <= 0` (return current mark, zero shares) before computing the ratio.

hypotheses.title: updateCoordinator leaves old coordinator as an enabled market-factory signer when new coordinator equals zero
hypotheses.description: `SolverVault.updateCoordinator(newCoordinator)` calls `marketFactory.updateSigner(coordinator, false)` then `updateSigner(newCoordinator, true)` before calling `super.updateCoordinator(newCoordinator)`. If `newCoordinator` is `address(0)` (or if `coordinator` and `newCoordinator` are the same address), the signer enable/disable pair is applied to the zero address or a no-op, and the vault's `coordinator` is set to that value. There is no check that `newCoordinator != address(0)` and no check that the previous signer was actually disabled. A zero coordinator makes `rebalance` and any `onlyCoordinator` path permanently unavailable, and leaves `marketFactory.signers[account][0]` enabled, allowing any zero-signer path (e.g. signature recovery edge cases) to be treated as a signer for the vault account.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner (or an operator abusing a mis-set role) calls `updateCoordinator(address(0))`; the vault's coordinator becomes zero, `onlyCoordinator` paths are bricked, and the enabled-signer entry for `address(0)` persists.
hypotheses.impact: Loss of vault rebalancing capability (DoS of coordinator functions) and a stale/incorrect signer authorization entry for the vault account.
hypotheses.recommendation: Revert when `newCoordinator == address(0)` or `newCoordinator == coordinator`, and assert `marketFactory.signers` reflects the intended final state before/after updating.

hypotheses.title: ChainlinkFactory._commitmentPrice can underflow/overflow when discount exceeds scalar
hypotheses.description: _commitmentPrice computes surchargedFee * (PERCENTAGE_SCALAR - discount) / PERCENTAGE_SCALAR. The discount comes from feeManager.s_subscriberDiscounts(...), which is external and attacker-influenced (subscribers can register high discounts). There is no check that discount <= PERCENTAGE_SCALAR. If discount > 1e18, PERCENTAGE_SCALAR - discount underflows and reverts, causing the whole commit() to fail for every keeper trying to commit that feed. Even if never >1e18, no clamp means a misbehaving/upgraded fee manager DoSes commits.
hypotheses.attackPath: A subscriber registers a >100% discount for their (this factory's) underlyingId; then every call to _parsePrices -> _commitmentPrice reverts with arithmetic underflow, blocking commits for that feed.
hypotheses.impact: Denial of service of the commit function for affected oracles, preventing oracle price updates and market settlement, which can freeze vaults/markets relying on that oracle.
hypotheses.recommendation: Clamp discount to PERCENTAGE_SCALAR (or validate discount <= PERCENTAGE_SCALAR) before subtraction.

hypotheses.title: Vault._settle() uses context.latestCheckpoint but stores it back at _checkpoints[context.global.latest] (off-by-one overwrite)
hypotheses.description: In the while loop, after nextCheckpoint is loaded from _checkpoints[context.global.latest + 1], the code calls context.global.processGlobal(context.global.latest + 1, ...) but then stores nextCheckpoint into _checkpoints[context.global.latest] instead of _checkpoints[context.global.latest + 1]. This overwrites the old checkpoint slot with the newly-completed checkpoint, while context.latestCheckpoint is set to nextCheckpoint. On the next iteration, _checkpoints[context.global.latest + 1] is looked up where context.global.latest has been updated to nextCheckpoint position; the freshly stored data in the lower id may be used elsewhere (totalAssets, _maxDeposit read _checkpoints[_accounts[address(0)].latest]) creating an inconsistency between stored index and intended checkpoint.
hypotheses.attackPath: Ordinary operation with more than one pending checkpoint (e.g., multiple settle() calls in different timestamps) causes checkpoint data for ids to be shifted; convertToShares/convertToAssets and _maxDeposit then read a checkpoint at the wrong id, giving incorrect share/asset conversion for subsequent users.
hypotheses.impact: Mis-accounting of share issuance/redemption and deposit limits, potentially enabling share inflation or allowing a user to deposit when unhealthy or claim more assets than fair.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store nextCheckpoint into _checkpoints[context.global.latest + 1] (or the appropriate id) after incrementing; align index with read/lookup.

hypotheses.title: Vault._settleUnderlying ignores revert/return of `market.settle` for each market
hypotheses.description: `_settleUnderlying` loops over markets calling `market.settle(address(this))` and ignores return values; more importantly if any registered market's `settle` reverts (or is paused), the whole vault function reverts. Because the loop runs before `_loadContext` and before user logic in every entry point (`settle`, `rebalance`, `update`), a single problematic market bricks all vault operations.
hypotheses.attackPath: Register a market that can be made to revert `settle` (e.g., an oracle with a paused/expired provider), or a market whose `settle` calls into an external oracle that reverts. Any user then cannot deposit/redeem/claim because every Vault entry point calls `_settleUnderlying`.
hypotheses.impact: Core functions (deposit, redeem, claim, settle) become unavailable, locking funds in the vault.
hypotheses.recommendation: Handle individual market settlement failures (try/catch or skip on failure), or otherwise document that one market's failure can DoS the vault.

hypotheses.title: MultiInvoker.invoke(account, ...) allows any operator to act on account but _claimFee and EXEC_ORDER honor arbitrary nested account
hypotheses.description: `_invoke(account, invocations)` is guarded by `onlyOperator(account, msg.sender)`, but inside the loop, `EXEC_ORDER` decodes `(address execAccount, IMarket market, uint256 nonce)` and passes `execAccount` to `_executeOrder(execAccount, market, nonce)`. The `onlyOperator` check is on the outer `account`, not on `execAccount`. `_executeOrder` calls `_marketSettle(execAccount)` and `_update(execAccount, ...)` which calls `market.update(execAccount, ...)` — acting on positions of `execAccount`. The keeper fee is charged to `execAccount` via `_raiseKeeperFee` (`_marketWithdraw(market, execAccount, raisedKeeperFee)`) and interface fees are deducted from it. Thus any operator of any account A can drive operations on an unrelated account B by passing `execAccount = B` in an EXEC_ORDER invocation, including triggering a withdrawal of B's collateral when B has a placed trigger order. The same applies to the invocation action bytes: `CLAIM_FEE` uses `account` (correct), but `EXEC_ORDER` uses `execAccount` (unchecked).
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker becomes operator of account A (their own or any account they control). Calls `invoke(A, [EXEC_ORDER(B, market, nonce)])` where B has an open trigger order that is fillable. The order executes against B's position and B pays the keeper fee and interface fees; attacker may also gain by front-running B's order or forcing unfavorable fill.
hypotheses.impact: Cross-account unauthorized position modification and fee deduction; a fillable trigger order for account B can be executed (and its fee charged to B) by anyone who is operator of any account, rather than only by B's operator or a keeper acting on B's behalf for fee compensation. Note that `EXEC_ORDER` is meant to be keeper-permissionless anyway; the concern is that the outer `account` used for the operator gate is decoupled from `execAccount`. Combined with the fact that keepers are permissionless via `_let`... see next.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require `execAccount == account || operator check on execAccount msg.sender` explicitly, or restrict EXEC_ORDER to keeper messaging only (e.g., disallow nested account).

hypotheses.title: `makerReceiveOnly` sign flip after funding computed from `toSkew` leaves wrong-side funding unflipped
hypotheses.description: In `_accumulateFunding`, `funding` is computed from the `pAccumulator` using `toSkew` (the position skew after applying the order), so its sign reflects the *next-period* skew. The `makerReceiveOnly` adjustment then compares `funding.sign()` to `context.fromPosition.skew().sign()` (the skew *before* the order) and flips `funding` when they differ. Because the funding rate was computed against `toSkew`, comparing and flipping against the pre-order `fromPosition.skew()` causes the wrong branch to be taken whenever the order changes the skew sign, flipping funding when it shouldn't (or failing to flip when it should). This inverts the maker's funding direction on skew-crossing orders, contrary to `makerReceiveOnly` intent.
hypotheses.attackPath: A trader submits an order that flips the market skew (e.g., from net long to net short) while `makerReceiveOnly` is true. `funding` from `accumulate` has sign matching `toSkew`, but the comparison uses `fromPosition.skew()` (opposite sign), so funding is negated. Makers then accrue funding with the wrong sign.
hypotheses.impact: Makers receive funding when they should pay (or vice versa) on skew-crossing versions, causing systematic value transfer between makers and takers.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compare `funding.sign()` against the sign of `toSkew` (the same skew used to compute funding), not `context.fromPosition.skew()`.

hypotheses.title: `OrderLib.sub` underflows before invalidation reconstructs order from guarantee
