hypotheses.description: In `_processOrderGlobal`, `context.pendingGlobal.sub(newOrder)` runs before `newOrder.invalidate(newGuarantee)`. `newOrder` at that point is read from `_pendingOrder[newOrderId]`, so subtraction should match what was added. However when `newOrderTimestamp > newOrder.timestamp` the code calls `newOrder.next(newOrderTimestamp)` first, then `pendingGlobal.sub(newOrder)` — after `next()` the order fields (makerPos, longPos, etc.) have been reset to zero, so `sub` subtracts a zero order from `pendingGlobal` (which contains the original non-zero order), leaving `pendingGlobal` out of sync with the sum of `_pendingOrder[id]` entries.
hypotheses.attackPath: Any pending order with an unfilled portion where the settlement oracle version is later than the order's timestamp triggers the `next()` path. `pendingGlobal` retains the order amounts that are never subtracted, while `_pendingOrder[id]` is stored with zeroed values by the subsequent store.
hypotheses.impact: The aggregate `pendingGlobal` accumulates stale size, then later `InvariantLib.validate` and `currentPositionGlobal.update(context.pendingGlobal)` operate on an inflated pending global, causing wrong margin/position checks and stuck/misaccounted pending orders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call `context.pendingGlobal.sub(newOrder)` before `newOrder.next(...)`, or subtract a cloned copy captured before the mutation.

hypotheses.title: `PositionStorageLocal.store` allows `direction` values > 2 that read as zero position
hypotheses.description: `PositionStorageLocalLib.store` computes `newValue.direction()` which returns 0, 1, or 2, and writes into a 2-bit slot. That's fine. But `read` interprets `direction == 0 => maker`, `==1 => long`, `==2 => short`, otherwise all zero. Since `direction()` is `self.long.isZero() ? (self.short.isZero() ? 0 : 2) : 1`, if a `Position` has both long and short nonzero (e.g. due to order accumulation or a partially-invalidated order leaving a both-sided state), `direction()` returns 1 and `magnitude = max(long, short, maker)` gets stored — the short side is silently dropped on store/read round-trip.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user's position ends up with both long and short nonzero due to `pendingOrders`/invalidate paths (see `OrderLib.invalidate` which can keep guarantee longPos and shortPos simultaneously if guarantee has both). On `_positions[account].store(...)`, the local position collapses to a single direction; the short side is discarded.
hypotheses.impact: User loses their short-side position silently; their accounted collateral/position mismatch breaks subsequent maintenance/margin checks and liquidation logic.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either enforce single-sided invariant in `PositionStorageLocalLib.store` (revert if both long and short nonzero) or use a slot layout that stores both sides.

hypotheses.title: RiskParameterStorageLib.validateAndStore checks uint24/uint48 ranges for some fields but not maintenance, makerFee/takerFee linear/prop, targetUtilization
hypotheses.description: `validateAndStore` explicitly range-checks `margin`, `minMargin`, `efficiencyLimit`, `makerLimit`, `pController.k`, `takerFee.scale`, `makerFee.scale`, `staleAfter`. It does not check `maintenance`, `takerFee.linearFee`, `takerFee.proportionalFee`, `takerFee.adiabaticFee`, `makerFee.linearFee`, `makerFee.proportionalFee`, `utilizationCurve.minRate/maxRate/targetRate/targetUtilization`, `pController.min/max`, `liquidationFee`, or `minMaintenance` against their storage bit widths — though `validate` bounds them indirectly via `protocolParameter.maxFee` etc. If `protocolParameter.maxFee`/`maxRate` are themselves greater than the storage widths, values that pass `validate` can be silently truncated by the `<<`/`>>` masking in `store`, and the coordinator who reads back with `read` sees different values than they intended. For example `pController.min`/`max` are stored as `int32` (`<= 214748%`), but `validate` only bounds `.abs()` by `protocolParameter.maxRate`; if `maxRate` is set beyond `2^31`, a larger value passes and is truncated on store. On read, `updateRiskParameter` re-reads the new parameter (`newRiskParameter = _riskParameter.read()`), so any invariant that relied on the coordinator-set value now uses the truncated one. This masks misconfiguration but can still allow an out-of-range bound to pass through if protocol upstream doesn't cap.
hypotheses.attackPath: Coordinator sets `pController.min = maxRate` just above the `int32` range (if `maxRate` > int32 max), the value passes `validate`, gets truncated on store to a smaller magnitude; downstream `_accumulateFunding` uses the truncated range. Practically requires `maxRate` mis-set, so it is more of a defense-in-depth finding.
hypotheses.impact: Silent truncation of risk parameters to values not intended by the coordinator; P-controller / utilization curve can behave outside configured envelope.
hypotheses.recommendation: Range-check every field that is packed in the storage library within `validateAndStore` (maintenance, all fee fields, min/maxRate, all P-controller fields, target utilization) against their exact bit widths before masking.

hypotheses.title: Fee-on-transfer tokens break collateral accounting in Market update/claim paths
hypotheses.description: `_update()` pulls collateral with `token.pull(msg.sender, ...)` and pushes with `token.push(...)`, assuming the exact amount moves. If the settlement token ever behaves like a fee-on-transfer/rebasing token (the market `token` is user/configurable via `definition.token`), the protocol's internal `Local` collateral can exceed or fall short of actual token balances. Likewise `claimFee` and `claimExposure` push `UFixed6` amounts that assume exact transfer. The internal ledger (`context.local.update(newOrder.collateral)`, `newGlobal.protocolFee`, etc.) is decremented by the nominal amount regardless of what actually moved. This creates a mismatch where the contract can become insolvent or a user can withdraw more than they deposited/earned.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Market deployed/configured with a fee-on-transfer token. 2) User deposits X; ledger credits X but contract receives X-fee. 3) User withdraws/closes; ledger debits X and pushes X, draining other users' collateral until contract balances run out. With a negative-fee token (rebasing up) the reverse allows over-accounting of others.
hypotheses.impact: Insolvency of the market; users' collateral/fee claims cannot be honored.
hypotheses.recommendation: Measure actual balance delta on pull and push (balanceOf before/after) and credit/debit the actual received/sent amount, or explicitly restrict the settlement token to a standard non-fee-on-transfer ERC20 at factory level.

hypotheses.title: KeeperOracle.settle reverts permanently for versions committed as unrequested (asyncFee == 0)
hypotheses.description: In `_commitUnrequested`, the stored `PriceResponse` has `syncFee = 0` and `asyncFee = 0`. Any account that registered a callback for that timestamp (via `request` → `_localCallbacks[currentTimestamp].add(account)`, which is added before the `requests[_global.currentIndex] == currentTimestamp` early-return) still lives in `_localCallbacks[version]`. Later `settle(version, maxCount, receiver)` iterates those callbacks and calls `market.token().push(receiver, UFixed18Lib.from(priceResponse.asyncFee))` with asyncFee = 0.
hypotheses.attackPath: `Token18.push` withdraws the token, which reverts if balance/allowance is below the amount or if the token disallows zero transfers. Even if it doesn't, the loop removes callbacks but each iteration pushes a zero amount, so the keeper receives no incentive; more critically, if the token (e.g. a standard ERC20 that doesn't revert on zero) is fine, the path is benign — but if `Token18.push` short-circuits with a revert on 0 (or amount exceeds the tiny dust pulled in), the entire `settle` loop wedges and callbacks can never be cleared, blocking `_localCallbacks[version]` from emptying.
hypotheses.impact: Settlement callbacks for unrequested/expired versions may be permanently unprocessable and their fees never paid; attackers can register callbacks on such versions cheaply (just by opening a position) to grief the keeper.
hypotheses.recommendation: Skip the `token().push` when `asyncFee == 0` (or remove the callback without a push), and only register callbacks for versions that will be requested.

hypotheses.title: PowerHalf.payoff reverts or produces garbage for prices above ~1.8e68, and loses sign of input
hypotheses.description: `Math.sqrt(UFixed18.unwrap(price.abs()) * BASE)` multiplies by 1e18 in 256-bit arithmetic. Any `price.abs()` above `type(uint256).max / 1e18` (~1.15e59) overflows and reverts; more subtly, the result is wrapped back via `Fixed18Lib.from`, which negates nothing, so the sign of the input price is discarded (`price.abs()`), unlike the other payoff providers that either preserve sign or operate on positive prices. The oracle's price field is a signed `Fixed6` (PriceResponse stores `int64 price`), so a negative price reaches `payoff` and the returned value is always non-negative.
hypotheses.attackPath: A price feed returning a negative price (e.g. spread, funding, or a compromised/misbehaving underlying) is converted to a positive payoff, so the market settles positions with the wrong payoff, allowing positions that should be unprofitable to be profitable and vice-versa.
hypotheses.impact: Mis-accounting in settlement; positions can be paid out incorrectly, allowing value extraction from the market by the position that benefits from the sign flip.
hypotheses.recommendation: Either validate `price >= 0` and revert on negative prices, or return `price.isNegative() ? result.neg() : result`; and pre-check the overflow bound before multiplying by `BASE`.

hypotheses.title: commit() advances latestVersion without ensuring monotonic ordering, enabling stale/late commits to regress state
hypotheses.description: `_commitUnrequested` guards `oracleVersion.timestamp <= _global.latestVersion`, but `_commitRequested` has no such guard. When `version.timestamp == next()`, the branch is taken unconditionally and then `_global.latestVersion = uint64(version.timestamp)` is assigned. If the requested timestamp is behind an already committed unrequested version (which is allowed because `_commitUnrequested` rejects timestamps >= next() only while next() != 0, but the ordering between a previously committed future unrequested version and a later requested version isn't enforced), latestVersion can move backwards, and `_responses[oracleVersion.timestamp]` for a version at or below the current latest is overwritten.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Commit an unrequested version at timestamp T2 while no request is pending. 2) Later a request is made and next() returns T1 < T2. 3) Commit requested T1 sets `_global.latestVersion = T1`, regressing below T2 and overwriting `_responses[T1]` after downstream state was already settled against T2.
hypotheses.impact: Latest version regresses, responses at earlier timestamps are overwritten, downstream market settlement reads an inconsistent history leading to wrong PnL/fee accounting.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `commit`, require `version.timestamp > _global.latestVersion` before assigning `_global.latestVersion`, and reject requested commits older than the current latest.

hypotheses.title: Oracle.at() skips current epoch boundary (i > 0, not i >= 0), losing timestamp 0/lowest epoch lookup
hypotheses.description: The loop `for (uint256 i = _global.current - 1; i > 0; i--)` never considers `i = 0`, and underflows when `_global.current == 0` (though in practice current >= 1 after initialize). For timestamps that belong to epoch 0 (the initial provider), `at()` will incorrectly walk back to the *current* provider or stop before epoch 1 and use `oracles[_global.current].provider.at(timestamp)` — returning the wrong provider's response (often a zero/invalid version). Also the loop condition `i > 0` means epoch 1 is never downgraded from the current, which is fine, but the missed epoch 0 is a real hole for historical lookups during updates.
hypotheses.attackPath: Query `at(timestamp)` where `timestamp <= oracles[0].timestamp`; the loop does not check epoch 0, so the current provider handles the call instead of the original one, returning wrong/zero data.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect historical price returned; downstream settlement at stale timestamp can settle at wrong price, causing loss.
hypotheses.recommendation: Iterate down to and including index 0, and handle `_global.current == 0` (return early or use the current provider directly).

hypotheses.title: KeeperOracle.commit() order: settle() before state write allows callback reentrancy on fees
hypotheses.description: `commit()` calls `market.settle(address(0))` and `oracle.claimFee(...)` and `market.token().push(receiver, ...)` after `_responses[version.timestamp].store(...)`, but `_global.latestVersion = uint64(version.timestamp)` is set *before* these external calls. Any callback triggered by `market.settle` (via market callbacks to accounts) or by the token push can observe the already-advanced `latestVersion` and reenter `settle()` (which checks `_global.latestVersion < version`) on an un-settled callback set for the previous version, causing overlapping settlements of fee payouts (`market.token().push(receiver, asyncFee)`) before the async fees were validated/consumed. Depending on the token (ERC777-like) the callback can loop.
hypotheses.attackPath: During `commit()`, an attacker-controlled market/account callback reenters `KeeperOracle.settle()` with a prior version; `latestVersion` has already advanced so the check passes; async fees are paid multiple times against the same fee base.
hypotheses.impact: Excessive fee payout / drain of async fee balance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reentrancy guard on `commit` and `settle`; update `_global.latestVersion` only after external calls have completed.

hypotheses.title: Controller._updateRebalanceGroup delete-then-recreate allows re-adding a market to a different group when redeclared in same message
hypotheses.description: The function first deletes the existing group by iterating `groupToMarkets[owner][message.group]` and deleting `marketToGroup`, then iterates `message.markets` and reverts if `marketToGroup[owner][message.markets[i]] != 0`. Because deletion happens against the *new* group's old contents, but `marketToGroup` is keyed per market, a market previously in the group being rewritten is cleared — fine. However, if the same market appears twice in `message.markets`, the first iteration sets `marketToGroup != 0` and pushes to `groupToMarkets`, and the second iteration sees `currentGroup != 0` and reverts — so duplicates in the same message are caught. The gap is that a market present in a *different* group cannot be moved: the code reverts rather than removing it from the other group, and `groupToMarkets` for that other group is never cleaned. This leaves stale entries (a market can appear in `groupToMarkets[owner][other]` with `marketToGroup==0`), so later `checkGroup`/`_rebalanceGroup` on the old group iterate a market whose config was deleted (target zero), returning `canRebalance` based on zero-target branch and transferring that market's entire collateral out of it.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner legitimately configured market M in group 1. Owner creates group 2 including M → reverts (blocked). No direct move. The exploitable variant: after delisting M from group 1 (group 1 rewritten without M), M can be added to group 2; but if group 1 was *not* rewritten, `marketToGroup` still points to 1. The realistic path is group 1 itself being rewritten each time, so leftover iteration is limited. The concrete bug is a revert-blocked market move plus stale configs where a market remains in `groupToMarkets` of another group after `_rebalanceConfigs` for that group/market was deleted (only the rewritten group's configs are cleared).
hypotheses.impact: A market's config can be deleted while it stays in another group's `groupToMarkets`, so a later rebalance of that group sees a zero target and `RebalanceLib.checkMarket` computes `imbalance = -marketCollateral` and (if > maxFee) withdraws the entire collateral from the market — forced full market exit the owner did not intend.
hypotheses.recommendation: When a market is added to a group, remove it from any previous group's `groupToMarkets`/configs (or forbid cross-group moves explicitly and ensure no stale entries remain), and validate that every `groupToMarkets` entry has a corresponding config.

hypotheses.title: TriggerOrder storage side is uint8 checked against type(uint8).max, defeating validation
hypotheses.description: In `TriggerOrderLib.store`, `newValue.side` is a `uint8`, so `if (newValue.side > type(uint8).max)` is always false and never reverts. The only effective side restriction is in `MultiInvoker._placeOrder`, which checks `order.side > 3`. But `TriggerOrderStorageLib.store` itself is the reusable guard for persisted orders and is advertised as external-safe; any caller path that reaches `store` without going through `_placeOrder` (e.g. future additions to MultiInvoker or other libraries) will persist arbitrary side values 0–255. Side values other than 0–3 then flow into `execute`, which only handles 0,1,2 and 3; any other value returns collateral=0 and does nothing to the position while still having fee>0.
hypotheses.attackPath: A caller places an order where `side` is, say, 4 via any path that bypasses the `_placeOrder` check (or the check is later loosened). `store` accepts it because `uint8` cannot exceed `type(uint8).max`. `execute` then does nothing to maker/long/short and returns zero collateral, yet `_executeOrder` still pays the keeper fee via `_handleKeeperFee` from the account.
hypotheses.impact: A trigger order that cannot change position but charges a keeper fee can be executed against an account by any keeper; the fee is withdrawn from the account's market collateral (`_raiseKeeperFee`), reducing the owner's collateral with no trade. Depending on how side is used, the order can never be meaningful but still drains collateral.
hypotheses.recommendation: Validate `newValue.side <= 3` explicitly in `store` (and in any path reaching it), and require `side` to be one of 0..3 before paying a fee in `_executeOrder`.

hypotheses.title: Trigger execute/interface fee uses market.update with zero collateral, so fees are drawn from account without margin re-check
hypotheses.description: `executeOrder` first charges the interface fee via `_chargeInterfaceFee` -> `_collateralAccountWithdraw(account, feeAmount)` which calls `controller.chargeFee` before `order.execute` runs the market update. The trigger order then submits `market.update(... Fixed6Lib.ZERO ...)`. Nothing in `executeOrder` verifies that the account remains sufficiently collateralized after the fee withdrawal and the position change; the keeper fee is likewise charged in `_raiseKeeperFee` outside the market's margin invariant. Since trigger orders are not "protected" orders, the market's `InvariantLib` margin check applies to the order, but the controller-side withdrawal happens separately and the trigger-order flow has no post-fee margined check.
hypotheses.attackPath: User places a trigger order whose execution plus the interface fee (percentage of notional, `notionalValue`) drains much of their collateral. When the trigger fires, the fee is withdrawn first, then the position update is applied; if the resulting position is under-margined, the market may revert on update, but the fee withdrawal ordering and separate controller ledger can leave the account in an inconsistent/under-margined state between the two calls, or the interface fee (percentage of notional) can exceed what the user expected, since only `order.maxFee` limits keeper fee, not interfaceFee.
hypotheses.impact: Interface fee can overcharge relative to what user can afford; account may become under-margined / revert after fee withdrawal, and percentage fee is uncapped by maxFee.
hypotheses.recommendation: Enforce `interfaceFee` bounds on placement and deduct/verify the fee within the same atomic margin check (performing the fee charge after market.update in the settled state, or checking collateral after both).

hypotheses.title: _raiseKeeperFee pulls DSU via controller.chargeFee without checking account collateral or triggering market settle; can revert or drain unexpectedly
hypotheses.description: `_raiseKeeperFee` decodes `(market, account, maxFee)` and computes `raisedKeeperFee = min(calculatedAmount, maxFee)`. It then calls `_collateralAccountWithdraw(account, raisedKeeperFee)` -> `controller.chargeFee(account, amount)`. This withdraws from the user's collateral account, but there is no check that `account` has enough in the collateral account, and the `market` decoded is only used to satisfy the `Keep` interface; the charge occurs on the controller, not the market. Because `_handleKeeperFee` is called after the order execution and after `_orders[...].store(order)` with `isSpent = true`, a failure in `controller.chargeFee` will revert the whole transaction, but if it succeeds when the account has insufficient collateral it may under-collateralize or, where the controller uses market withdrawal including pending settlement, can charge an amount that causes the account to enter liquidation unwisely.
hypotheses.attackPath: Keeper executes a trigger order whose keeper fee (buffered) exceeds the account's free collateral; `controller.chargeFee` is called with the computed amount. Depending on controller implementation, this either reverts (DoS of the trigger order execution) or drains the collateral beyond a safe margin.
hypotheses.impact: Trigger orders can be made unexecutable (DoS) if fee > collateral, or account becomes under-margined after keeper fee.
hypotheses.recommendation: In `_raiseKeeperFee`/`_chargeInterfaceFee`, cap fee to a value that keeps the account margined, and use the decoded `market` to settle and validate before withdrawing, or keep fees within an explicit per-order budget.

hypotheses.title: Manager.executeOrder pays keeper from account collateral after the order without re-validating collateral feasibility
hypotheses.description: executeOrder() computes whether the order can execute (checkOrder), then calls _chargeInterfaceFee(...) and order.execute(...) to settle and update the account, then calls _handleKeeperFee(keepConfigBuffered, ...) which calls _raiseKeeperFee() -> controller.chargeFee(account, raisedKeeperFee). Neither the interface-fee charge nor the keeper-fee charge validates that the account retains sufficient margin after those charges; _collateralAccountWithdraw just calls controller.chargeFee, and the underlying Account allows the charge as long as DSU is present in the collateral account, not as long as the position is still margined. The order can therefore be executed with a withdrawal that de-margines the account and leaves it below maintenance.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user places a trigger order with a large interfaceFee or maxFee such that executing at the trigger price (where collateral is just barely sufficient) removes a substantial portion of collateral. Keeper executes; _chargeInterfaceFee / _handleKeeperFee pull DSU from the account after Market.update; the account is now under-margined and the next liquidator can seize the position at the user's expense, or if the collateral account lacks sufficient funds the execution reverts, blocking trigger.
hypotheses.impact: Account can be pushed below maintenance immediately after a legitimate order execution, enabling liquidation griefing or blocking of trigger execution near liquidation thresholds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute interface and keeper fees up-front (using maxFee and interfaceFee), include them in the pre-execution feasibility check (or re-check maintenance after the charges), and cap the fee withdrawals to the free collateral of the account.

hypotheses.title: Referral fee paid from collaterized account even when order is exempt via guarantee
hypotheses.description: In `_accumulateFee` the `takerTotal` is reduced by `guarantee.takerFee` before computing the trade fee, but `takerSubtractiveFee` is computed as `takerFee.muldiv(order.takerReferral, takerTotal)` with the reduced `takerTotal`. When a guarantee fully exempts the taker portion (`takerTotal == 0`), `takerSubtractiveFee` is forced to zero even though `order.takerReferral` may be non-zero. More significantly, when partial exemption occurs, the referral amount is not scaled down to the guaranteed size, so the subtractive fee portion (and thus referral payout accumulated via `subtractiveFee`) is over- or under-reported relative to the fee actually paid by the taker.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user places an order via a solver/guarantee that exempts most taker size from fees (`guarantee.takerFee` close to `order.takerTotal()`). The order still carries a large `takerReferral`. `_accumulateFee` computes `takerSubtractiveFee` against the small residual, inflating subtractive fee per unit of charged fee. `subtractiveFee` feeds `CheckpointAccumulationResponse`, which the Market uses to credit referrers.
hypotheses.impact: Mismatched referral accounting lets referrers collect fees disproportionate to trade fees actually charged, or conversely causes guarantees to undercharge; either way value is shifted between referrers, market, and taker.
hypotheses.recommendation: Scale `order.takerReferral` (and `guarantee.solverReferral`) proportionally to `takerTotal / order.takerTotal()`, or compute subtractive fee against the full `order.takerTotal()` and reserve the exempt portion explicitly.

hypotheses.title: ChainlinkFactory._parsePrices does not verify Chainlink report validity or expiry for all feeds, allowing any signed report to be replayed for any `version`
hypotheses.description: `_parsePrices` calls `chainlink.verifyBulk` and only checks `feedId == toUnderlyingId[ids[i]]`, then builds `PriceRecord(observationsTimestamp, price, cost)` using the report's `observationsTimestamp`. It never checks that the reports correspond to the requested `version`, nor that `observationsTimestamp` values are unique/consistent across reports. `_validatePrices` in `KeeperFactory` only checks `observationsTimestamp` is within `[version + validFrom, version + validTo]`, and the keeper can supply any set of reports. Because `verifyBulk` returns whatever reports were passed in (assuming the Chainlink verifier validates them as genuine reports), an attacker can batch old reports that happen to fall in the window for a `version` the keeper is trying to publish.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker obtains old verified reports (e.g., from a previous `verifyBulk` call or the Chainlink API) whose `observationsTimestamp` falls within `[version + validFrom, version + validTo]`, then calls `KeeperFactory.commit(oracleIds, version, data)` with those reports. Since `_commitmentPrice` is recomputed from `nativeQuantity`, the `cost` differs from the original, but the `price` and timestamp check pass, committing a stale price for a `version` at which the market should have a fresh price.
hypotheses.impact: Maker/solver vaults use `market.oracle().latest().price` and `checkpoint(...)`; committing stale prices through the factory can be used for value extraction (e.g., causing `_toAssets`/`_toShares` to mispricing redemptions) or to force incorrect liquidation/settlement.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require each report's `observationsTimestamp` to equal (or be 0 for) the requested `version`, or enforce uniqueness and monotonicity per feed, and reject reports older than the last committed version.

hypotheses.title: Vault._socialize has no protection against `context.totalCollateral < context.global.assets` and uses `min` to reduce claims, over-crediting remaining holders
hypotheses.description: `_socialize` returns `claimAssets * min(totalCollateral, global.assets) / global.assets`. When `totalCollateral < global.assets` (a vault that has lost value), a partial payout ratio is applied, but the global account's `assets` is decremented by the full `claimAssets` in `context.global.update(...)`; only the reduced `claimAmount` is pushed to the user. The difference (undelivered assets) is not re-attributed to the remaining global assets, so calling `update` multiple times by many holders progressively reduces the aggregate claimable value without reducing `global.assets` proportionally.
hypotheses.attackPath: A vault becomes undercollateralized (e.g., due to market losses). Each holder calls `update(account, 0, 0, claimAssets)`. Each call decrements `global.assets` by `claimAssets` but pays only `claimAssets * totalCollateral / global.assets`. After the first holder, the ratio `totalCollateral/global.assets` is unchanged, but the sum of undelivered value accumulates in `global.assets` and is orphaned.
hypotheses.impact: A portion of users' redeemable value becomes permanently unclaimable (stranded in the accounting), because `global.assets` is decremented by the pre-socialization amount rather than the delivered `claimAmount`.
hypotheses.recommendation: Decrement `global.assets`/`local.assets` by the delivered `claimAmount` and leave the shortfall in `global.assets` for further reductions.

hypotheses.title: SolverVault.updateCoordinator can silently mis-authorize signers when previous coordinator was zero
hypotheses.description: `updateCoordinator` unconditionally calls `marketFactory().updateSigner(coordinator, false)` before setting the new coordinator. `MarketFactory.updateSigner` toggles whether `msg.sender` (the signer) is registered for the vault account; disabling a never-configured `address(0)` or disabling an existing coordinator while the new one is set to the same address causes state churn. More importantly, the call to `updateSigner(coordinator, false)` happens before `super.updateCoordinator(newCoordinator)` and, if `newCoordinator == coordinator`, the net effect disables the signer used by the current coordinator.
hypotheses.attackPath: An owner sets `updateCoordinator(x); updateCoordinator(x)` (or the coordinator reuses the same address) and observes that after the second call the coordinator is disabled as a signer in `MarketFactory`, breaking all coordinator-signed intents. If `coordinator == address(0)` a spurious `updateSigner(address(0), false)` occurs.
hypotheses.impact: Vault coordinator loses signing capability (DoS of solver operations) or admin tools end up disabling an unrelated signer; can strand funds if coordinator is needed to close/rebalance.
hypotheses.recommendation: Guard against `newCoordinator == coordinator` and `coordinator == address(0)`; only disable the old signer if it differs from the new one.

hypotheses.title: SolverVault.rebalance moves collateral without settling markets, letting coordinator front-run settlement
hypotheses.description: `rebalance` directly calls `from.update`/`to.update` on the underlying markets and never calls `_settleUnderlying()` for those markets or the vault's `_settle`. Underlying markets settle at oracle versions; executing taker orders on `from`/`to` before the next vault settlement lets the coordinator choose the order book state and prices at which the vault's checkpoint collateral will be valued. Unlike every other stateful vault entry point (`settle`, `rebalance(address)`, `update`), which all start with `_settleUnderlying()`, this function does not enforce that markets are settled or that the vault's local positions are current.
hypotheses.attackPath: Coordinator observes an unfavorable incoming market move, calls `rebalance` to shift collateral between markets via taker orders before `_settleUnderlying` runs at the next version, so the vault's realized checkpoint reflects the manipulated position rather than the strategy's intended allocation.
hypotheses.impact: Coordinator can systematically realize losses for the vault and gains for themselves/third parties across markets by controlling timing of collateral moves.
hypotheses.recommendation: Call `_settleUnderlying()` and settle/checkpoint the vault before executing the transfer, and constrain `amount` by each market's current strategy target.

hypotheses.title: SolverVault.rebalance() bypasses accounting/pause and can be reentered or abused to shift collateral arbitrarily
hypotheses.description: rebalance(IMarket from, IMarket to, UFixed6 amount) directly calls from.update(address(this), 0, -amount, 0) then to.update(address(this), 0, +amount, 0) with no call to _settleUnderlying() or checkpoint settlement, no pause modifier, and no verification that the vault's target collateral distribution is maintained. The two market calls are external and could reenter (markets call back into token interactions). It is not guarded by whenNotPaused, unlike every other state-changing Vault entrypoint, and it lets the coordinator move collateral between markets arbitrarily, undercutting the minMargin/ineligible accounting the base Vault assumes is computed at settle time.
hypotheses.attackPath: Coordinator (or a compromised coordinator) moves collateral out of a market whose leverage/margin then becomes insufficient; because Vault._manage always recomputes using _settleUnderlying() and local collateral from markets, inconsistencies surface as VaultCollateralOutOfSync or revert during withdrawals. Additionally if a registered market is upgraded or malicious, the two external update calls between which the vault has 0 collateral in `from` can be reentered.
hypotheses.impact: Collateral can be moved in ways the strategy logic would reject, potentially leaving a market under-margined; combined with no pause guard, coordinators can continue operating while paused.
hypotheses.recommendation: Add whenNotPaused, call _settleUnderlying() first, and validate resulting leverage against registration constraints.

hypotheses.title: Vault.update() calls asset.pull before _manage and asset.push; token callbacks allow reentrancy into vault accounting
hypotheses.description: In _update(), after mutating global/local/checkpoint memory structures, asset.pull(msg.sender, deposit) performs an external token transfer, then _manage(...) calls external market.update() on every registered market (which can transfer tokens and call back), and finally asset.push(msg.sender, claimAmount). The in-memory context is only persisted in _saveContext after these external calls complete, so a reentrant call to update()/settle()/rebalance() during the token callback or market callback will read stale on-chain storage (context.global, context.local, current checkpoint not yet stored) and overwrite the outer call's unsaved changes. Tokens with transfer hooks (ERC777, ERC1363) or malicious markets can trigger this reentrancy.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker crafts deposit token with a transfer hook (if the vault asset allows) or exploits a market's update callback; the hook reenters Vault.update() with claimAssets != 0 to read pre-update global.assets/deposit; upon return, the outer save overwrites local state, allowing the inner caller to escape with inflated claims or to skip deposit accounting.
hypotheses.impact: Double-spend of claimAssets or loss of deposit accounting; possible theft from vault or accounting desync between checkpoint, accounts and market collateral.
hypotheses.recommendation: Persist state and/or add nonReentrant before external pull/update/push calls; save context before external interactions.

hypotheses.title: Intent update mutates position/collateral accounting before the payer's token transfer but accounts receiver's leg as if settled
hypotheses.description: `_updateIntent`/`_updateMarket` create a `newOrder` with `Fixed6Lib.ZERO` collateral for the intent flow, so no token movement occurs and the intent legs are recorded purely against pending orders/guarantees. However, `_update` is invoked twice per `update(...)` call (solver leg and trader leg), each doing a full `_loadForUpdate`/`_settle` cycle. The first leg can advance `local.currentId`/`global.currentId` and settle pending orders, so the second leg operates against already-advanced state within the same transaction, and the `guarantee` from `GuaranteeLib.from` is applied with the referrer/`chargeTradeFee` flags independent of the counterpart leg. This allows the two legs to be accounted under different settlement contexts, which can cause the trader and solver legs to receive differing pending-state treatment in a single call.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker submits a `Fill`/intent where the solver's account and trader's account settle into different versions in the same call; the first `_updateIntent` advances the id and settles, the second sees the new currentId. No guarantee of atomic counterparty pricing exists between the two legs.
hypotheses.impact: Counterparty legs of an intent fill can be settled at different (mismatched) accumulated states, mispricing one side and transferring value between accounts.
hypotheses.recommendation: Load a single settlement context and apply both legs atomically against the same version/state, or prevent the first leg from advancing/finalizing state used by the second leg within one transaction.

hypotheses.title: `claimExposure` trusts `newGlobal.exposure` and pushes/pulls without bounds
hypotheses.description: `claimExposure()` reads `newGlobal.exposure`, and depending on sign either `token.push` (market pays owner) or `token.pull` (owner pays market), then resets exposure to zero. There is no check that the market actually holds enough tokens for `token.push`, and no check that the pull amount matches accrued exposure (only trusts the stored state). If `exposure` accumulated a positive value that exceeded actual market balance (e.g., because `VersionLib._accumulateAdiabaticFee`/`_accumulateAdiabaticExposure` credited exposure in ways not paired with value movement), the push would drain general market liquidity or revert.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner calls `claimExposure()` after a series of trades that miscredited `exposure` (e.g., zero-maker paths that set `adiabaticExposureMarket = adiabaticExposureMaker` — see below). `token.push` transfers `exposure.abs()` from market to owner, pulling funds from underlying collateral that belongs to other accounts.
hypotheses.impact: Misappropriation of market collateral by the owner when exposure bookkeeping overstates positive exposure.
hypotheses.recommendation: Reconcile exposure against token balance, and only permit pulls (owner funds) when balance is insufficient; audit `_accumulateAdiabaticExposure` sign logic.

hypotheses.title: `_accumulateAdiabaticExposure` sets market exposure equal to maker exposure when maker is zero, then resets to zero
hypotheses.description: When `context.fromPosition.maker.isZero()`, the code sets `adiabaticExposureMarket = adiabaticExposureMaker` (which is `-adiabaticExposure`), then immediately sets `adiabaticExposureMaker = adiabaticExposureMaker - adiabaticExposureMarket` → `0`. So in the zero-maker case the maker stream gets zero and the market absorbs the full exposure. However `next.makerValue.increment(adiabaticExposureMaker=0, maker=0)` is a no-op, but the market's `exposure` (via `_response`) increases, and `claimExposure` pays the owner. This is the intended fallback, but the maker exposure is silently discarded even if `fromPosition.maker == 0` yet `fromPosition.long/short` non-zero — meaning the taker side exposure isn't captured at all; `adiabaticExposure` should still be netted against maker stream but is instead moved to market.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker does a large taker trade while maker == 0 (e.g., after all makers exit), creating substantial `adiabaticExposure`. Owner then calls `claimExposure()` to extract the profit that was intended to be socialized to taker positions.
hypotheses.impact: Value that should compensate takers (or offset losses) is instead claimable by the owner; not socialized back to taker streams.
hypotheses.recommendation: Route market exposure to the taker value streams when maker == 0, or do not credit market exposure at all for the taker path.

hypotheses.title: `updateBeneficiary` does not reset/route existing market exposure or fees
hypotheses.description: `updateBeneficiary` just sets `beneficiary`. There is no hook to migrate or reconcile pending `global.exposure` or `global.protocolFee` that may be conceptually attributed to the old beneficiary. Since `claimExposure` is owner-only (not beneficiary-only) and `claimFee(account)` credits `factory().owner()`, the beneficiary setter has no effect on fund routing — but the beneficiary address is expected to receive donations; any external integration (per the codebase) relying on `beneficiary` for exposure/donation payouts may route incorrectly. In this file there's no payout to `beneficiary` at all, so the setter appears to be a no-op that could be misleading.
hypotheses.attackPath: N/A within shown code except that `beneficiary` is set but never used for any transfer; external assumptions aside.
hypotheses.impact: Medium only if downstream code depends on `beneficiary` receiving exposure/donations which doesn't happen here.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove or wire up the `beneficiary` usage, or document that it's informational.

hypotheses.title: update(account, ...) overloads with address(0) signer skip authorization for msg.sender-self paths but the 4-arg account/maker/taker path uses address(0) signer while others use msg.sender, inconsistent operator gating
hypotheses.description: The `update(address account, Fixed6 amount, address referrer)` overload passes `msg.sender` as `signer` into `_updateMarket`, which calls `IMarketFactory.authorization(context.account, msg.sender, signer, orderReferrer)`, so `operator` == `msg.sender` == `signer`. However `update(address account, Fixed6 amount, Fixed6 collateral, address referrer)`, `update(address account, Fixed6 makerAmount, Fixed6 takerAmount, Fixed6 collateral, address referrer)`, and `update(address account, UFixed6 newMaker, UFixed6 newLong, UFixed6 newShort, Fixed6 collateral, bool protect[, address referrer])` pass `address(0)` as signer. The authorization result is consumed downstream in InvariantLib (not shown) and MagicValueLib; if the invariant library relies on `updateContext.signer` being a valid signer for `account`, then the `address(0)`-signer variants bypass signer verification and permit any caller to update any account's position/collateral as long as `msg.sender` is authorized as an operator (or in some configurations possibly less). The inconsistency between overloads means the security semantics differ. Depending on factory authorization semantics, the zero-signer path could be exploitable to move another user's position when the invariant layer checks only `operator`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker observes that `update(account, amount, collateral, referrer)` passes signer=address(0); if InvariantLib's protection/margin validation relies on `updateContext.signer` being nonzero for certain operations (e.g. protected orders), attacker calls this overload targeting a victim account with a self-authorized operator config (or via operator that is not the victim). 2) Alternatively attacker registers as operator via factory (if allowed) and uses the zero-signer overload to bypass signer checks that the `msg.sender`-signer overload applies.
hypotheses.impact: Unauthorized position or collateral changes on another user's account, leading to loss of funds/liquidation.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure all overloads pass a consistent signer (`msg.sender` for self-updates) and that `InvariantLib`/`MagicValueLib` require a valid signer for operations on behalf of another account; do not use `address(0)` signer for account-affecting updates.

hypotheses.title: Settlement fee charged per order in _accumulateSettlementFee, but _accumulateLiquidationFee charges fee * settlementFee * liquidationFee irrespective of maker position, potentially over-charging
hypotheses.description: `_accumulateLiquidationFee` computes `liquidationFee = toOracleReceipt.settlementFee.mul(riskParameter.liquidationFee)` and decrements it per oracle version regardless of whether any account is actually being liquidated in that version. `_accumulateSettlementFee` divides the receipt fee across `orders = order.orders - guarantee.orders`; but `_accumulateLiquidationFee` uses the full `settlementFee` for every version processed, including versions with zero maker/taker activity, and credits it unconditionally to `next.liquidationFee` even for non-liquidation versions. It accumulates a hypothetical liquidation fee per version with `decrement(..., ONE)`, so per-version it adds `settlementFee * liquidationFee`. This value is later consumed by `CheckpointLib._accumulateLiquidationFee` (not shown) to credit liquidators. The mismatch in base (orders vs ONE) and unconditional apply means the liquidator referral payout is derived from values that can be accrued even when no order was settled for that version (if `toOracleReceipt.settlementFee` is nonzero from other flows), leading to over-credit relative to fees actually collected and mis-accounting.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Attacker is registered liquidator (or referrer) of an account's order. 2) Either oracle-requested settlement fee is nonzero on versions with no maker/order activity, or sequence occurs where settlementFee is set but orders==0. 3) `next.liquidationFee` accrues `settlementFee * liquidationFee` while no corresponding settlement fee was deducted, and on liquidation the liquidator is credited based on this inflated accrued value, draining market/other users' funds.
hypotheses.impact: Excess payouts to liquidators at the expense of market makers/users; long-term insolvency.
hypotheses.recommendation: Only accumulate the liquidation fee when there is a real order/liquidation in the version (guard `liquidationFee` on `liquidationFee != 0` and orders > 0), and use consistent normalization basis with settlement fee accounting.

hypotheses.title: Oracle.at, status, latest mis-report fees for versions in callback-period with stale latest
hypotheses.description: `Oracle.at(timestamp)` selects the provider by walking epochs, but `KeeperOracle.at(timestamp)` returns a receipt whose settlement fee equals `_responses[timestamp].syncFee + asyncFee * _localCallbacks[timestamp].length()`. `commit()` computed that fee with the callback count at commit time, but callers re-querying `at` later see the fee size with the current (post-settlement) callback count — because `settle()` removes entries from `_localCallbacks`, `at` for an already-settled version reports a smaller settlement fee than was actually paid, and for un-settled versions it reports fees that will be paid out again per settle call.
hypotheses.attackPath: A market reads `at(version).receipt.settlementFee` after settlement to update accounting for keeper incentives; it sees `syncFee` only (since callbacks were removed), so its recorded fee differs from what was charged to the market at `commit`.
hypotheses.impact: Market-level accounting diverges from paid amounts; repeated reads of `at` are not idempotent, so integrations using `at` for settlement accounting can mis-account fees across epochs.
hypotheses.recommendation: Persist the settlement fee (or the callback count used) in the `PriceResponse` at commit time and have `toOracleReceipt` return that stored amount rather than recomputing from the mutable callback set.

hypotheses.title: PythFactory._parsePrices does not override as non-view and forwards msg.value; combined with KeeperFactory.create type, parsePriceFeedUpdates min/max range allows arbitrary old publishTime
hypotheses.description: `_parsePrices` calls `pyth.parsePriceFeedUpdates{value: msg.value}` with `minPublishTime = type(uint64).min` and `maxPublishTime = type(uint64).max`, so any historically valid Pyth update (including arbitrarily old prices) is accepted. `PriceRecord.publishTime` is set from `parsedPrices[i].price.publishTime` and this value flows into `_validatePrices`/`_transformPrices` in KeeperFactory (not shown) to determine the version. Because there is no lower bound tied to the requested version, a keeper can feed a stale but correctly signed Pyth update, potentially settling an outdated price.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) Keeper obtains any previously published Pyth update payload for the underlying id. 2) Calls `KeeperFactory.commit` with that stale `data`. 3) `_parsePrices` accepts it since range is unbounded; `publishTime` reflects the old price.
hypotheses.impact: Prices from arbitrary past times can be used to settle versions, distorting oracle versions that markets rely on for settlement.
hypotheses.recommendation: Constrain `minPublishTime`/`maxPublishTime` around the requested `version` (e.g., within the granularity window) so only fresh updates are accepted.

hypotheses.title: `request` indexes callbacks by `current()` and reuses `_global.currentIndex`, allowing request slot desync across markets
hypotheses.description: `request` is callable by the oracle for any market, but `_localCallbacks[currentTimestamp]` is keyed only by timestamp, not by market. Multiple markets sharing one KeeperOracle instance (stated as supported in the header) will interleave callbacks into the same set, and `commit`/`settle` will call `market.settle(account)` on `oracle.market()` for every account regardless of the market that requested. Since `oracle` is the only market bound, and the oracle is per market in `Oracle.sol`, this may be restricted; but the `settle` loop iterates the shared callback set and calls `market.settle(account)` for accounts that may not be registered on that market, causing reverts that block settlement.
hypotheses.attackPath: If two markets ever route through the same KeeperOracle (per the documented support), the second market's requests add accounts to the shared callback set; on `settle`, `market.settle(account)` reverts for accounts unknown to `oracle.market()`, blocking async fee payouts.
hypotheses.impact: DoS of settlement callbacks and stuck async fees.
hypotheses.recommendation: Key `_localCallbacks` by `(market, version)` or ensure per-oracle single market invariant is enforced.

hypotheses.title: Array indexing overflow in DedupLib when duplicates span indices
hypotheses.description: The dedup logic sets `indices[i] = indices[index]` where `index = _match(ids, i)` is the first occurrence. If a later duplicate index refers to an earlier element that was itself a duplicate of an even earlier one, `indices[index]` is fine only if `index < i` and already processed. Correct. However the `duplicates` counter is incremented for every non-first occurrence, and `dedupedIndex = i - duplicates`. This yields a contiguous index only if duplicates appear in monotone non-decreasing order of the underlying identity; the pack array itself is compact but `indices` mapping of the *first* occurrence might point to a deduped index that is later overwritten. E.g., [A, B, A]: i=2 matches index 0, so `indices[2] = indices[0] = 0` — fine. But [A, B, C, B, A, D] type patterns can cause `indices[i]` of an earlier element to be assigned before that element's final deduped index is set, yielding wrong indices. The caller depends on dedup indices mapping to the deduped array, so incorrect indices corrupt downstream price attribution.
hypotheses.attackPath: Caller (factory) passes data array with duplicate oracle IDs interleaved so that `_match` returns an index whose `indices[]` entry is stale/wrong; downstream `_transformPrices` uses the wrong ID for a price and applies the wrong price to a market.
hypotheses.impact: Wrong price applied to a market id, potentially incorrect settlement.
hypotheses.recommendation: Fix index mapping by storing the deduped index for the first occurrence and always assigning `indices[i] = indices[matched]` after that first entry has been finalized; verify with tests.

hypotheses.title: RebalanceLib target uses groupCollateral * target after partial withdrawals, enabling keeper to over-drain a thin market
hypotheses.description: `checkMarket` compares `marketCollateral` against `targetCollateral = groupCollateral.mul(target)` and computes `imbalance = targetCollateral - marketCollateral`, returned as the amount `_rebalanceGroup` passes to `account.marketTransfer(market, imbalance)`. In `_rebalanceGroup`, withdrawals are done first using these imbalances (negative sign), then deposits with the positive ones. But `_settleMarkets`/`checkGroup` are called before any transfers, so the imbalances are based on pre-move collateral. After the first loop drains surplus markets, the second loop still pushes the same precomputed positive imbalances, which were sized against the old `groupCollateral`. As collateral moves out of surplus markets into the account, the deficits remain exactly as computed and are funded from the account, so the totals reconcile; however, if a surplus market's `marketCollateral` was exaggerated by unsettled locals or by `withdraw` having already pulled DSU, `imbalance` can exceed what the account holds, causing `marketTransfer` to fail (DoS) or, in the zero-target branch, to withdraw the entire market.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner sets a low-threshold config and a `maxFee` near the imbalance level. Keeper calls `rebalanceGroup`; checkMarket returns full-drain imbalance for any market whose target computed to zero (e.g. groupCollateral=0 edge or target=0) or large imbalances from stale locals; the two-pass transfer loop then attempts to move more than available, reverting the whole rebalance, or drains the thin market fully (zero-target branch: `imbalance = -marketCollateral`).
hypotheses.impact: Keeper-triggered full withdrawal of a market's collateral, or a revert that blocks the rebalance (griefing / denial of the rebalance function).
hypotheses.recommendation: Recompute market collateral per-market after each transfer (or cap each transfer by the account's available DSU), and explicitly handle the zero-target and zero-groupCollateral cases in the rebalance loop rather than transferring the whole market at once.

hypotheses.title: Rebalance withdrawal loop can push more collateral into a deficit market than account actually holds
hypotheses.description: `_rebalanceGroup` first pulls `imbalances[i]` from surplus markets and then pushes `imbalances[j]` into deficit markets. But the surplus pull is a market `update` with negative collateral, which does not necessarily deliver exactly `imbalances[j]` DSU to the Account — the amount pushed later is the desired target, not the amount actually withdrawn. `Account.marketTransfer` in `Account.sol` calls `wrapIfNecessary` only when the amount is positive, and if insufficient DSU exists for a push, the loop still attempts it, causing the market to pull more than was received (pulling any other DSU the account holds, or reverting). There is no check that the sum of pulls is at least the sum of pushes before the push loop runs.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner sets a group where one market is in surplus and another is in deficit. Between `_settleMarkets` and the pull loop, the surplus market's collateral can be reduced (e.g. price movement/settlement loss or pending position update), so the actual pulled DSU is less than `imbalances[j]`. The push loop then attempts to push the full deficit amount into the deficient market, draining the account's other collateral or reverting the entire rebalance with no compensation when the account lacks DSU.
hypotheses.impact: The account ends up with market collateral that doesn't match its target; either other market positions or idle DSU are unexpectedly drawn down, or a paid keeper's `rebalanceGroup` reverts. Persistent mismatch between `checkGroup` imbalances and what is actually transferred undermines the group collateral accounting that withdrawals/market transfers rely on.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the actual amount withdrawn from each surplus market (DSU balance delta) and only push up to that amount, or cap each push by the DSU actually received, reverting if the total pushed exceeds pulls.

hypotheses.title: RebalanceLib threshold check compares percent against raw target when target collateral is small
hypotheses.description: `checkMarket` computes `targetCollateral = groupCollateral.mul(Fixed6Lib.from(marketConfig.target))` and then `pctFromTarget = Fixed6Lib.ONE.sub(marketCollateral.div(targetCollateral))`. When `groupCollateral` is small (e.g. after most collateral is drained to a deficit market or the owner has small balances), `targetCollateral` rounds toward zero (Fixed6 fixed point), making `marketCollateral.div(targetCollateral)` overflow or produce an enormous value. There is no minimum-target guard analogous to the `targetCollateral.eq(Fixed6Lib.ZERO)` branch. When `targetCollateral` is zero but not equal to zero due to precision, the division produces an unbounded `pctFromTarget`, and `canRebalance` becomes true even for negligible imbalance.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner configures a market with a tiny non-zero `target` (e.g. 1e-6) and the group's total collateral shrinks so `groupCollateral * target` rounds to zero. A caller calls `rebalanceGroup`: `targetCollateral` is 0 and `imbalances[i]` returns `-marketCollateral`, which may be larger than `maxFee`, so an unwanted full withdrawal from that market occurs. If `targetCollateral` rounds to a very small non-zero value, the division can produce a huge pct and also cause overflow/revert.
hypotheses.impact: Markets with small target allocations can be fully emptied unexpectedly, or `checkGroup`/`rebalanceGroup` can revert due to overflow, blocking rebalances. This is a keeper-triggered move of owner collateral that doesn't correspond to the configured target.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use the same zero-target guard on `targetCollateral` after the multiply, and cap/validate `marketConfig.target` against a minimum absolute amount (e.g. require target collateral above a dust threshold) before dividing.

hypotheses.title: MultiInvoker EXEC_ORDER keeper fee charged to account even when caller not authorized on that account - permissionless execution mis-design
hypotheses.description: Even if `_invoke`'s EXEC_ORDER is intended keeper-permissionless, `_executeOrder` has no `onlyOperator`-style check. It calls `_handleKeeperFee` charging `account` (any `execAccount`), then `_marketSettle(account)` and `_update` on `account`. Combined with `_raiseKeeperFee`, which pulls the fee from the account via `_marketWithdraw`, any caller of `invoke(X, [EXEC_ORDER(victim, ...)])` — where X is any account they can be operator of or their own — forces fills on the victim's trigger order and charges the keeper fee / interface fee to the victim. While trigger-order execution is designed to be keeper-callable, the review target is that it's reachable via the operator-gated `invoke` without any check tying `execAccount` to authorization.
hypotheses.attackPath: As above.
hypotheses.impact: Forced fills at keeper's discretion; forced fee extraction.
hypotheses.recommendation: Same as above; validate `execAccount` matches outer `account` or enforce a dedicated keeper path.

hypotheses.title: Account.marketTransfer uses UNCHANGED_POSITION magic passes but never validates market is a real Market; token==DSU check only
hypotheses.description: Only check that `market.token() == DSU`. A fake market can implement `token()` returning DSU and `update(...)` that simply does nothing or emits; it cannot move funds unless it has approval — which `Account.marketTransfer` grants via `DSU.approve(address(market))`. Combined with the previous finding (persistent unlimited approval), a user-signed `MarketTransfer` to an arbitrary address grants that address unlimited DSU spending power on the account. The user must sign a message containing the market address, so this is self-inflicted, but combined with the approval persistence it lets a user "deposit" once to a fake market (no-op pull is not called in Account.marketTransfer — the fake market's `update` implements the pull itself) and the fake market can pull more later. Since a signed message authorizes a specific market address, this remains user error. However `getAccountAddress` / `verifyMarketTransfer` uses `common.account`, and `verifyMarketTransfer` does not bind `market` to `marketFactory.instances`, so **relayed** signature flows can suggest a malicious market to a signer whose signer authorization is broad — attacker creates a market address with DSU token and gets a signature? Not in code shown. Low confidence.
hypotheses.attackPath: n/a
hypotheses.impact: n/a
hypotheses.recommendation: Add `marketFactory.instances(market)` check in `_marketTransferWithSignature` before calling `account.marketTransfer`.

hypotheses.title: RebalanceLib.checkMarket division by targetCollateral when groupCollateral or target negative can produce misleading imbalance; and with negative targetCollateral (groupCollateral negative) pctFromTarget sign flips
hypotheses.description: `targetCollateral = groupCollateral.mul(target)`. If `groupCollateral` is negative (net debt) and `target > 0`, targetCollateral is negative. Then `pctFromTarget = ONE - marketCollateral.div(targetCollateral)`. Fixed6 division by a negative yields negative result; `pctFromTarget.abs()` may compare on assumption that it's a fraction of target but a negative `targetCollateral` reverses the meaning of surplus/deficit, and `imbalance = targetCollateral - marketCollateral` sign may not correspond to "deposit/withdraw". Also when `groupCollateral == 0` with non-zero target, `targetCollateral == 0`, handled; when `marketCollateral == 0`, `pctFromTarget = ONE`, and `canRebalance = ONE - 0 > threshold` → true if threshold < 1 always true, `imbalance = targetCollateral`. This leads `_rebalanceGroup` to deposit into markets whenever group collateral is nonzero and any market is empty; but if groupCollateral came from a market with a positive target of 0 elsewhere, could cause withdrawing from a market to empty markets repeatedly on each call, but each call is bounded. The division produces incorrect rebalancing when group collateral becomes negative (possible if position losses exceed collateral? in `locals(owner).collateral` signed could be negative). Rebalance would then try to transfer positive amounts to reduce "deficit" incorrectly, potentially depositing funds into the wrong market.
hypotheses.attackPath: A keeper calls `rebalanceGroup` after group collateral is net-negative (losses). `checkMarket` mislabels surplus/deficit; the two-pass loop pulls from markets the code believes have surplus but actually have deficits — `marketTransfer(market, imbalance)` with negative imbalance withdraws, possibly reverting due to insufficient collateral or, worse, succeeding when it shouldn't, concentrating collateral in the wrong market.
hypotheses.impact: Collateral misallocation; possible revert of rebalance (DoS) or loss through bad allocation.
hypotheses.recommendation: When `groupCollateral` is not positive, treat the group as un-rebalancable or define behavior explicitly; guard `targetCollateral.gt(0)` and skip division on non-positive groupCollateral.

hypotheses.title: verifyAction exposed without domain binding to message type, enabling signature reuse across action types
hypotheses.description: `verifyAction` proves that `action.common.signer` signed the `Action` struct, and `validateAndCancel` consumes the nonce. Every other message (`MarketTransfer`, `Withdrawal`, `RebalanceConfigChange`, relayed messages) embeds `Action` and is hashed with a structure-specific type hash. Because `verifyAction` is a public verifier whose sole purpose is to validate an `Action`, a signature the owner provides "as" a nonce-cancelling or generic action can be consumed by anyone via `verifyAction`, burning the nonce so the intended structured message (which reuses the same nonce, since signed offline) reverts as already-cancelled. Because the EIP-712 domain is shared with all the structured messages, the signer's only protection is the user signing each message type separately; but nonces are global per signer, and `verifyAction` lets a third party front-run any pending signed message's nonce.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner signs `Withdrawal{..., common.nonce = N}` off-chain and submits, but a watcher sees the pending tx in the mempool. Watcher calls `verifyAction(action)` with the same `common` (the `Action` sub-struct) and its own copy of the signature—wait, they need a signature over `ActionLib.hash(action)`, which differs from `WithdrawalLib.hash`. If the owner has also signed any bare-`Action` message (e.g. a nonce-cancellation relayed to the verifier uses the signer's own `CancelNonce` on the core verifier, so this path is limited)—the vector that remains: `verifyAction` lets anyone consume the signer's nonce via a signature intended for a `MarketTransfer`'s embedded `Action`? No, different hash. The exploitable path is: any time the signer signs a bare `Action` (e.g. as part of `RelayedNonceCancellation`'s `action.common`, whose hash equals `ActionLib.hash` for the `action` field—these can be extracted), an observer can consume the nonce before the intended structured use.
hypotheses.impact: Griefing: a pending signed message from a user can be made to revert (nonce consumed) by an attacker who extracts a signature over a bare `Action`, blocking withdrawals and market transfers without spending the owner's funds.
hypotheses.recommendation: Remove the public `verifyAction` entrypoint or make it only callable by the controller/account and verify it is invoked in a context where re-consuming a nonce twice cannot lock out other action types; alternatively namespace nonces per message type.

hypotheses.title: updateOperatorWithSignature/updateSignerWithSignature allowself-signed messages only, contradicting legitimate custody setups but blocking operator recovery
hypotheses.description: Both `updateOperatorWithSignature` and `updateSignerWithSignature` require `operatorUpdate.common.signer == operatorUpdate.common.account`. This makes the delegated-signer route useless for any account whose `common.account` is a smart-contract wallet or multisig without `isValidSignature` support via an EOA signer (Verifier uses `SignatureChecker.isValidSignatureNow` against `common.signer`, which here is forced to equal `account`), and more seriously, it means updates are only authenticated by the account's own signature; but `_updateOperator` is called with `operatorUpdate.common.account` in place of the caller, so any party holding a valid account signature can flip an arbitrary operator address on that account.
hypotheses.attackPath: An attacker who is a delegate and can obtain the account's EOA signature for any message (e.g., through a phishing/relaying channel that already has the signer's signature for a similar struct with an unused chain) can craft an `OperatorUpdate` with `accessor = attacker` and `approved = true` and satisfy the equality check.
hypotheses.impact: Given a leaked account signature, an attacker becomes an operator with full position/collateral control; also blocks legitimate multi-signer setups entirely (functionality denial for custody accounts).
hypotheses.recommendation: Allow `common.signer` to be an authorized signer of `common.account` via `_authorized`/`signers` mapping rather than requiring strict equality, and gate the operator update against the signer's authorization.

hypotheses.title: KeeperOracle/DedupLib and PriceResponse declarations not shown; TriggerOrder.notionalValue fee-accounting uses market oracle not the executed price and misprices percentage interface fee
hypotheses.description: `notionalValue` reads `market.oracle().latest().price` and multiplies the absolute price by `self.delta` (or the current position when closing). `_chargeInterfaceFee` in Manager uses this value for percentage fee orders, charging based on the latest price rather than the price at which the trigger order actually executes within `order.execute`, and computing notional on the raw `delta` even for closing orders that clamp against actual position. This lets a fee be charged that is inconsistent with the realized notional change of the market update, undercharging or overcharging the interface fee and thus the receiver's `claimable`.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user places a percentage interface-fee order with a large `delta`, then before execution the market price jumps; the fee charged is based on the old/latest price, not the actual executed notional — the receiver claims a mismatched amount, and the account's collateral is debited accordingly.
hypotheses.impact: Over/under-charge of interface fees relative to the true position change; the receiver may claim more DSU than the fee the user intended to pay.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute the notional change after applying the pending position and the delta to a resulting position and multiply by the oracle price used at execution (or the price the market will use), not `self.delta` times the latest price when closing.

hypotheses.title: Manager store()/executeOrder does not verify that manager's claimable/fee withdrawal leaves user with non-negative collateral; fee charged before order execution
hypotheses.description: `executeOrder` calls `_chargeInterfaceFee` before `order.execute` and before the market update; `_collateralAccountWithdraw` calls `controller.chargeFee` with the computed fee. The market update inside `order.execute` will reduce collateral further via new trade fees, so the account can wind up negative-collateralized after the fee + market update, and the interactive collateral check in `InvariantLib.validate` is bypassed because the action is a market update to close/reduce. This allows the interface fee to push the user's account into deficit when combined with the market-side fees, with the loss ultimately borne by the protocol via liquidation shortfall.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user with the minimum viable collateral places a trigger order with an interface fee equal to near their whole equity; on execution, fee is withdrawn, then market update subtracts trade fee and settles PnL, driving collateral below zero without the invariant being enforced.
hypotheses.impact: Interface fee receivers or keepers extract DSU beyond the user's risk capacity; residual bad debt socialized to other market participants.
hypotheses.recommendation: Check the user's resulting collateral after all charges and reject the execution (or account for the fees in the market update) to guarantee non-negative collateral before the fee receiver is credited.

hypotheses.title: Trigger order placement allows overwriting an unspent order with maxFee increase but does not prevent replacing an order with larger delta/side mismatch
hypotheses.description: `_placeOrder` only rejects if `old.isSpent`, otherwise it allows the same `orderId` to be overwritten as long as `order.maxFee >= old.maxFee`. There is no check that the replacement order has the same fields (side/delta/price), so any party who can pass `placeOrder` for `account` (the account itself) can replace the order's content after it was signed/committed. More importantly, the `_placeOrder` for `placeOrderWithSignature` uses `request.action.common.account` as the account, so a signed request to place a specific `TriggerOrder` can be front-run by the *account owner* with a `placeOrder(market, orderId, arbitraryOrder)` overwriting the signed order, but also a signer-authorized relayer can only place; that's fine. The real gap is there is no replay/replacement protection across `placeOrder` and `placeOrderWithSignature` sharing the same `_orders[market][account][orderId]` slot combined with only `isSpent` being checked.
hypotheses.attackPath: An account or its signer signs a `PlaceOrderAction`; before it is relayed, the account owner (or an operator) calls `placeOrder` with the same `orderId` and a different trigger order. The signed relay then overwrites the owner's just-placed order (allowed because `old.isSpent` is false and `maxFee` check only enforces non-decreasing). Unexpected replacement of persisted orders can destroy intended orders.
hypotheses.impact: Owners can have arbitrary signed orders overwritten/canceled by unauthorized replacement with the same orderId; potential for griefing/DoS on persisted trigger orders and unexpected execution.
hypotheses.recommendation: Require replacement orders to also preserve the nonce/timestamp or reject overwriting a non-empty order unless the caller is the account owner/operator, or require the replacement to be a signed action as well.

hypotheses.title: Local claimable credited on Match but never reduced when account's DSU is withdrawn from market to pay keeper/interface fee via controller — check
hypotheses.description: In `executeOrder`, `_chargeInterfaceFee` increases `claimable[receiver]` by `feeAmount` and calls `controller.chargeFee(account, feeAmount)` to pull the DSU from `account` into the manager. `_raiseKeeperFee` also calls `controller.chargeFee(account, raisedKeeperFee)` but notably, the keeper fee amount is *not* credited anywhere—it is presumably forwarded by `_handleKeeperFee` to the keeper. If `controller.chargeFee` transfers DSU directly to the manager contract, then `claimable[receiver]` mirrors the manager's internal balance. But `claim` for a receiver unwraps and pushes from the manager's *own DSU balance* without checking that `claimable[receiver]` <= manager's actual DSU balance. If the manager's DSU is also used for other things (e.g., it holds DSU transiently during keeper fee flows), a claim could drain DSU belonging to a different pending fee. Also `_raiseKeeperFee` withdrawal lands in the manager and is then paid to the keeper via the `Keep` base, but there is no guarantee that `claimable` + kept balance do not double count / overdraft the manager's DSU.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) A large interface fee is charged, `claimable[receiver] += X`, DSU in manager += X. 2) Meanwhile a trigger executes and `_raiseKeeperFee` pulls DSU of amount Y from account and it sits in manager before pushing to keeper (same tx so not exploitable) — but if `claimable[receiver]` > manager DSU because of a controller.chargeFee that transfers less than expected or fails silently, `claim` reverts or sends wrong funds. More importantly, if `controller.chargeFee` debits `account` but does NOT transfer DSU to the manager (e.g., controller pays out directly or charges on a different ledger), `claimable[receiver]` would overstate the manager's DSU balance, letting an early claimer drain DSU that is not claimed.
hypotheses.impact: Claimable overstatement may drain manager DSU that belongs to keeper compensation or other claimable balances, or make later claims revert.
hypotheses.recommendation: Credit claimable only after confirming DSU bytes arrived in the manager (measure balanceBefore/after), and enforce `claimable[*]` sum <= manager DSU balance invariant.

hypotheses.title: AccountLib.processLocal credits shares/assets but doesn't verify Checkpoint is at or after the user's local.current timestamp
hypotheses.description: `processLocal` unconditionally sets `self.latest = latestId` and performs `toAssetsLocal`/`toSharesLocal` against the given checkpoint. In `Vault._settle` it is called only when `context.latestTimestamp >= nextCheckpoint.timestamp`, but `nextCheckpoint` is `_checkpoints[context.local.current]`; the guest checkpoint used is fetched by `context.local.current` (an id), whereas `processGlobal` uses `nextCheckpoint.deposit`/`redemption` for its own `latest + 1` id. Any mismatch between the id space used by `processLocal` and `processGlobal` (e.g., different ids after a cancellation or a fast path) would cause the local to be marked processed against a checkpoint that does not match the global.
hypotheses.attackPath: Through `update` with `redeemShares = UFixed6Lib.MAX` after a global process advances `global.latest` past `local.current`, then `processLocal` is invoked against a checkpoint that is farther ahead than intended; the user's pending deposit/redemption is converted with the wrong `deposit`/`redemption` counters.
hypotheses.impact: User shares/assets are converted with the wrong checkpoint, over- or under-crediting the user in a way that other LPs bear.
hypotheses.recommendation: Assert `checkpoint.timestamp <= context.latestTimestamp` and that `latestId` matches, and that the per-order counts agree with the called functions.

hypotheses.title: ChainlinkFactory._commitmentPrice reads nativeQuantity from wrong report field
hypotheses.description: `_parsePrices` decodes `verifiedReports[i]` into `(feedId, , observationsTimestamp, nativeQuantity, , , price)` and passes `nativeQuantity` to `_commitmentPrice(feedId, nativeQuantity)`. The report layout for Chainlink Data Streams is `feedId, validFromTimestamp, observationsTimestamp, nativeFee, linkFee, expiresAt, price`. Re-fee is charged by the Chainlink verifier, and the keeper cost charged to the keeper is derived from `nativeFee`, which is what the fee manager expects. If the report field being read is a stale/irrelevant integer (e.g., a timestamp), keeper rewards will be wildly wrong (too small or too large).
hypotheses.attackPath: A commit keeper submits reports; the parse emits wrong cost, causing the keeper to be over- or under-rewarded per commit. Front-running commit with stale reports can maximize mispricing.
hypotheses.impact: Keeper fee under/overcharging → keeper griefing, subsidy drain, or keeper failure to cover Chainlink fee.
hypotheses.recommendation: Verify the report tuple field positions against the deployed Chainlink verifier spec and decode the actual `nativeFee` field; validate by comparing against `feeManager.getFeeAndReward`.

hypotheses.title: Vault.register/updateWeights/updateLeverage/updateParameter rebalance against stale global state before mutating
hypotheses.description: `register`, `updateWeights`, `updateLeverage`, and `updateParameter` all call `rebalance(address(0))` before applying the new configuration. `rebalance(address(0))` runs `_settleUnderlying()` then `_loadContext(address(0))`, so it uses `context.global` and the *old* registrations/weights. That is acceptable for `rebalance` itself, but if the current `context.totalCollateral` is negative or markets are closed, `_manage` returns early and the configuration change is applied anyway. There is no check that the vault's accounting is consistent with market collateral after the update, meaning registration/weight changes can be applied while the vault is in an unhealthy position, and the subsequent settle will reconcile against different weights than what was used to produce the last checkpoint.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner changes weights while vault is in a negative-collateral or closed-market state; `_manage` in `rebalance` short-circuits (`if (context.totalCollateral.lt(Fixed6Lib.ZERO)) return;`), so markets are left at old allocations but the checkpoint was already snapshotted with the old configuration; the next `update`/`settle` rebalances using the new weights against a checkpoint whose `assets` reflect the old configuration.
hypotheses.impact: Temporary misallocation and potential loss to depositors/redeemers at the boundary between configuration change and settlement.
