hypotheses.recommendation: Revert configuration changes (or defer them) when `context.totalCollateral < 0` or any registered market is closed, so the checkpoint, registrations, and market collateral stay consistent.

hypotheses.title: totalAssets/totalShares subtract checkpoint redemption at current checkpoint price using stale deposits
hypotheses.description: `totalAssets()` computes `checkpoint.assets + checkpoint.deposit - checkpoint.toAssetsGlobal(checkpoint.redemption)`, and `totalShares()` computes `checkpoint.shares + checkpoint.toSharesGlobal(checkpoint.deposit) - checkpoint.redemption`. Both read from `_checkpoints[_accounts[address(0)].read().latest]`, i.e. the *latest completed* global checkpoint, but they then apply conversions for the *current* pending `deposit`/`redemption` of that checkpoint. During the interval between a user calling `update()` (which writes the current checkpoint with new `deposit`/`redemption`) and the next settlement, these view functions are used by `_maxDeposit`, `convertToShares`, and `convertToAssets`. Because `toSharesGlobal`/`toAssetsGlobal` apply `_settlementFeeForOrders` and `_withSpread` based on the checkpoint's *current* `deposit`, `redemption`, and `tradeFee`, the computed totals can diverge from what the vault will actually settle, and `_maxDeposit` can allow deposits that push past `maxDeposit` at settlement or reject valid ones.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user causes `context.currentCheckpoint.deposit`/`redemption` and `tradeFee` to change by calling `update`, then an integrator or another user reads `convertToShares`/`convertToAssets`/`_maxDeposit`; the resulting quote reflects a one-off adjustment that is then re-applied when settling, effectively double-counting or dropping the settlement fee portion.
hypotheses.impact: Incorrect share/asset quotes and deposit-limit checks, allowing users to deposit or redeem at a stale conversion rate and dilute other holders.
hypotheses.recommendation: Compute view functions from the last *settled* checkpoint without applying in-progress `deposit`/`redemption` spreads, or snapshot the conversion parameters per-order at `update` time.

hypotheses.title: KeeperFactory.commit() trusts msg.sender as keeper but pays reward for all oracles; partial revert leaves no cleanup
hypotheses.description: commit() iterates over oracleIds and calls IKeeperOracle.commit(...) on each oracle with msg.sender and costs[i]. Costs are computed in _commitmentPrice (via _parsePrices) using Chainlink fee manager per feed, but the factory ignores whether the underlying oracle instance exists or whether it is properly authorized. If any oracle's commit reverts (e.g. version already requested by someone else, or an oracle paused), the entire batch reverts and the keeper loses all gas. A malicious keeper cannot prevent a competitor from committing, but _validatePrices uses keeperOracleParameter validFrom/validTo and a keeper oracle could reject a commit for a version that has already been committed via a different path; there's no dedup at factory level, so any single oracle instance blocking reverts the whole multi-oracle commit. Conversely, if the oracle list has duplicates (matching oracleIds), _transformPrices applies costs and the same oracle.commit is called twice with the same version, letting the second call revert the entire batch.
hypotheses.attackPath: Attacker observes a keeper's pending commit for oracleIds containing a duplicate id (or an id whose version already exists); the keeper's transaction reverts and the keeper loses gas, allowing the attacker to front-run the actual commit at the correct version.
hypotheses.impact: Keeper griefing / DoS of commit path in the ordinary case of duplicate or already-committed oracleIds; keeper rewards and liveness suffer.
hypotheses.recommendation: Dedup oracleIds (not just underlyingIds) or skip already-committed entries; guard against duplicate oracleIds in the batch.

hypotheses.title: Vault._ineligible subtracts global.deposit minus new deposit from assets; pending deposits can be counted as eligible erroneously
hypotheses.description: _ineligible computes `context.global.deposit.sub(deposit)` and subtracts it from collateral, then adds back context.global.assets. For a deposit call (deposit>0), this treats the deposit amount as gone from pending deposit and thus available for allocation, but the pending global.deposit is the previous checkpoint's backlog which hasn't yet been settled; that backlog could exceed collateral, causing totalCollateral.unsafeSub(global.assets)... underflow / clamped wrongly. Because it is computed before global.deposit is updated, a withdrawer in the same transaction interacts with redemptions that include the not-yet-applied deposit, and the result feeds MakerStrategyLib.allocate which may revert if collateral < totalMargin.
hypotheses.attackPath: A user calls update with a small deposit while global.deposit > global.assets + totalCollateral - deposit, causing ineligible to underflow and allocate to revert, blocking all vault updates (DoS). Conversely a caller in the same checkpoint as a large prior deposit gets inflated eligible assets and can withdraw after dilution.
hypotheses.impact: Withdrawals/updates revert (DoS) or eligible allocation miscomputed, causing unfair dilution of existing depositors.
hypotheses.recommendation: Use safe subtraction and validate that global.deposit >= deposit; compute eligibility after applying the new deposit.

hypotheses.title: Exposure claiming lets owner pull from an account with insufficient token balance, but exposure may exceed actual claimable token collateral
hypotheses.description: `claimExposure` lets the owner (beneficiary) pull/push `newGlobal.exposure.abs()` tokens when the market's exposure is non-zero, without checking that the market's actual token balance backs that exposure. `claimExposure` resets `exposure` to zero and pushes tokens to owner. If exposure accrued was larger than actual token reserves held (fees may not have been realized into token balances), `token.push` reverts and exposure cannot be claimed, permanently locking the value or reverting.
hypotheses.attackPath: Owner calls `claimExposure` after exposure accrues; if the token balance is less than `exposure` (e.g., because fees were accrued but not yet claimed into the token balance with `claimFee`), the push reverts, blocking the reset and the claim.
hypotheses.impact: Exposure claim DoS, or if partially backed, it drains tokens that back other users' claimable fees/collateral, leaving claimers unable to withdraw.
hypotheses.recommendation: Ensure `claimExposure` accounts for the actual token balance backing and/or does not reset exposure in a way that lets it leapfrog other fee claims.

hypotheses.title: `KeeperOracle.commit` calls `market.settle(0)` which may pull from a sub-oracle not synchronized with `Oracle` epoch
hypotheses.description: `commit` invokes `market.settle(address(0))`, pulling the market forward using the KeeperOracle's `latest()` and `at()`. During an `Oracle` epoch switch (`_global.current != _global.latest`), `at()` routes older timestamps to the previous provider. If a previously-requested timestamp lies in the routed range but the version has been committed on this KeeperOracle, `at()` will not consult this contract; the price committed now may never be pulled into the market, while the keeper fee is charged.
hypotheses.attackPath: During epoch switch, price committed for a timestamp that resolves to the old provider; market ignores new price; keeper still gets paid and `latestVersion` advanced.
hypotheses.impact: Fee paid without serving a price; and the market may use a stale price.
hypotheses.recommendation: Block commit during epoch transition or ensure committed versions are consulted by `at()` for the new epoch too.

hypotheses.title: PlaceOrder max-fee monotonicity check can be bypassed by re-using an order id with an empty/full overwrite after spent flag races
hypotheses.description: `_placeOrder` blocks lowering `maxFee` only when the existing order is non-empty (`if (!old.isEmpty() && old.maxFee.gt(order.maxFee))`), and only blocks re-use when `old.isSpent`. However there is no ordering guarantee with respect to `executeOrder` — between `checkOrder` and storing `isSpent = true` in `executeOrder`, a new `placeOrder` for the same orderId can be inserted (the order was not yet marked spent). That replacement is later overwritten by `_orders[market][account][orderId].store(order)` inside `executeOrder` (the old TriggerOrder captured before execution gets stored). Result: a freshly placed replacement order (with a possibly higher `maxFee`/different intent) is silently dropped and marked as the previously-executed one, so the actor loses the new order's parameters and cannot reuse the id because the store sets `isSpent = true`.
hypotheses.attackPath: 1) User has trigger order A (maxFee 100) placed. 2) Keeper calls executeOrder. 3) Before the store of A.isSpent, an attacker (or the user) calls placeOrder for the same id with order B (higher maxFee, valid). 4) `_placeOrder` sees old = A (not spent, not empty), passes maxFee check, overwrites storage with B. 5) executeOrder continues, sets A.isSpent = true and stores A. Storage now shows A spent; B is lost, and further placeOrder with the same id is rejected forever.
hypotheses.impact: Legitimate replacement orders can be eaten during execution, and the orderId slot is permanently burned. Additionally, this enables MEV to cancel a user's intended-update by replacing then losing it.
hypotheses.recommendation: Store `isSpent` before calling `order.execute` (or store using a version/nonce increment), and make `_placeOrder` reject if orderId is pending-execution or handle-racing.
